The Grecians rally, and their powers unite.

A piston powered by hydraulic pressure.
An act of ramming.

ety: Borrowed from Arabic رَمَضَان (ramaḍān).

"mid-15 c., perhaps frequentative of 'romen' 'to walk, go' perhaps via 'romblen' (late 14 c.) 'to ramble.' The vowel change perhaps by influence of Middle Dutch 'rammelen,' a derivative…

ety: Borrowed from Japanese ラーメン (rāmen), from Mandarin 拉麵 /拉面 (lāmiàn, “pulled noodles”). Doublet of laghman, lamian, and ramyeon.

ety: From Middle French ramification, or its source, Medieval Latin rāmificātiō. By surface analysis, ramify + -ication.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French rempart (“rampart of a fort”), from Old French remparer (“to defend, fortify, inclose with a rampart”), from re- (“again”) + emparer (“defend, fortify, surround, seize, take possession of”), from Old Occitan amparer, from Vulgar Latin *anteparō (“to prepare”), from ante- + parō (“to prepare”).

a ranch or rancho owner

"Owen and she went raspberrying in the woods back of her farm," answered Anne. "They won't be back before supper time—if then."
[…] Mrs. Thrifty was picking pie cherries, two boys were raspberrying, and the fourth son, as I recall it, blueberrying.

s.def: A noise intended to imitate a fart, made by blowing air out of the mouth while the tongue is protruding from and pressed against the lips, or by blowing air through the lips while they are pressed firmly together or against skin (often a form of tickling) used humorously or to express derision.
A physically disabled person.
To make the noise intended to imitate the passing of flatulence.
raspy
ex: He spoke in a rasping voice due to throat cancer.

s.def: exasperating
Pushing forward with great force.
ex: Myhill gets fingertips onto it and helps the rasping drive onto the bar and over or a corner.
Celta then levelled following a crisp move between Daniel Wass, Guidetti and Orellana, the Chilean sending a rasping drive high beyond Casilla.
Zeki Amdouni had a rasping long-range drive parried away by David Raya

s.def: present participle and gerund of rasp
A sound that rasps.
The act of rasping as with a file.

ety: From Middle English raat, rat, ratt, ratte, rotte, from Old English ræt, rætt, from Proto-West Germanic *ratt, from Proto-Germanic *rattaz, *rattō (“rat”), of uncertain origin, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *Hreh₃d- (“to gnaw, scrape, scratch”). However, the rat may have been unknown in Northern Europe in antiquity, and the Proto-Germanic word may have referred to a different animal; see *rattaz for more. Attestation of this family of words begins in the 12th century. Cognates Cognate with…

s.def: A medium-sized rodent belonging to the genus Rattus.
Any of the numerous members of several rodent families that usually have short limbs, a pointy snout, a long, hairless tail, and a body length greater than about 12 cm, or 5 inches.
A person who is known for betrayal.
ex: Near-synonyms: rouge, scoundrel, snake; see also Thesaurus:villain
He’s more a man than any pair of rats of you in this here house.
What a rat, leaving us stranded here!

A scab: a worker who acts against trade union policies.
A person who routinely spends time at a particular location.
ex: Our teenager has become a mall rat.
He loved hockey and was a devoted rink rat.

s.def: A wad of shed hair used as part of a hairstyle.
A roll of material used to puff out the hair, which is turned over it.
Vagina, vulva.
ex: Get your rat out.

Poison used to kill rats and other rodents.

Alternative form of rateable

ety: From French ran tan plan, onomatopoeic.

To drum repeatedly.

ety: Unadapted borrowing from French ratatouille, from Occitan ratatolha (ratatouille is a dish originally from Nice, and is also found in Provence), French form from diminutive prefix tat- + touiller (“to stir”), from Latin tudiculō (“grind, mix”), from tudes (“hammer”), from Proto-Indo-European *tud-, from *(s)tewd-.

s.def: A traditional French Provençal stewed vegetable dish consisting primarily of tomatoes, zucchini and eggplant.

ety: From Middle English rate, from Old French rate, from Medieval Latin rata, from Latin prō ratā parte (“according to a fixed part”), from ratus (“fixed”), from rērī (“think, deem, judge, estimate", originally "reckon, calculate”).

s.def: The proportional relationship between one amount, value etc. and another.
ex: At the height of his powers, he was producing pictures at the rate of four a year.
Negative responses to this program were being received by the office of the National Gay Task Force at the rate of ten to one.

s.def: The relative speed of change or progress.
ex: The rate of production at the factory is skyrocketing.

s.def: The price of (an individual) thing; cost.
ex: He asked quite a rate to take me to the airport.

s.def: The worth of something; value.
ex: There shall no figure at such rate be set, / As that of true and faithfull Iuliet.
His natural parts were not of the first rate, but he had greatly improved them by a learned education.

s.def: Speed.
ex: The car was speeding down here at a hell of a rate.
Many of the horse could not march at that rate, nor come up soon enough.

s.def: A set price or charge for all examples of a given case, commodity, service etc.
ex: Postal rates here are low.

s.def: A wage calculated in relation to a unit of time.
ex: We pay an hourly rate of between $10 – $15 per hour depending on qualifications and experience.

s.def: Any of various taxes, especially those levied by a local authority.
ex: I hardly have enough left every month to pay the rates.

s.def: A class into which ships were assigned based on condition, size etc.; by extension, rank.
ex: This textbook is first-rate.

s.def: Established portion or measure; fixed allowance; ration.
ex: The one right feeble through the evil rate / Of food which in her duress she had found.

ety: From Middle English rather, from Old English hraþor, comparative of hraþe (“soon, early, fast”). More at rathe. Cognate with Dutch radder (“faster”), comparative of Dutch rad (“fast; quick”), German Low German radd, ratt (“rashly; quickly; hastily”), German gerade (“even; straight; direct”). By surface analysis, rathe + -er.

s.def: Used to specify a choice or preference; preferably, in preference to. (Now usually followed by than)
ex: I'd rather not have spent all the money, but it really was an emergency.
I would like this one rather than the other one.
I s'pose we'd better clean the kitchen, but we had much rather not do anything right now.

s.def: Used to introduce a contradiction; on the contrary.
ex: It wasn't supposed to be popular; rather, it was supposed to get the job done.
She didn't go along, but rather went home instead.

s.def: Somewhat, quite; to an unexpected degree.
ex: It's been rather/quite a good meal overall, but this melon is rather too tasteless.
We had some rather worse news today.
We’ll be seeing rather a lot of you over the next few days.

s.def: Introducing a qualification or clarification; more precisely. (Now usually preceded by or.)
ex: I didn't want to leave. Or rather I did, just not alone.

s.def: More quickly.
Prior; earlier; former.
ex: Now no man dwelleth at the rather town of Damietta.

s.def: An enthusiastic affirmation.
ex: Would you like some? –Rather!
"Do you mean to say, young man," she said frostily, "that you expect me to drink this stuff?" ¶ "Rather! Bucks you up, you know."

s.def: A choice or a preference.
ex: If I had my rathers I'd make up my own band. Art Blakey on the skins, Charlie Mingus on the bass, John Coltrane on the sax, Harry Edison on the horn-
I would rather do it by myself. I would rather, if I had my rathers, not be seen doing it.

s.def: To prefer; to prefer to.
ex: You'd rather us dead.

A pigeonhole.

s.def: To give formal consent to; make officially valid, to sign off on.
ex: They ratified the treaty.

s.def: present participle and gerund of rate
A position on a scale.
An evaluation of status, especially of financial status.
ex: They have a poor credit rating.

s.def: A number, letter, or other mark that refers to the ability of something.
ex: He has a high chess rating.

s.def: A quantitative measure of the audience of a television program.
ex: A rating, at best, is an indication of how many people saw what you gave them.

s.def: A seaman in a warship.
An enlisted seaman not a commissioned officer or warrant officer.
ex: In the Royal Navy the ratings, in order, are: ordinary seaman, able seaman, leading seaman, petty officer and chief petty officer.

ety: Borrowed from Latin ratiō. Doublet of ration and reason.

s.def: The relative magnitudes of two quantities (usually expressed as a quotient).
A number representing a comparison between two named things.
Ellipsis of ratio decidendi.
The number of comments to a post or other expression on social media relative to the number of likes; a high ratio suggests disagreement with the contents of the original post.
To respond to a post or message on social media in a greater number than the number of likes the post receives, especially to condemn or mock the original poster.
ex: The politician's post was quickly ratioed due to its controversial nature.
It used to be fun to watch tweets like that get ratioed back into their ugly corner of the internet.
Cue the goading Trump tweet (“Howard Schultz doesn’t have the ‘guts’ to run for President!”), the Twitter ratioing and the outrage from the left.

s.def: Indicates disagreement with a post the user disagrees with or dislikes.
ex: "Ratio. YoungBoy is better." "What?" "Make better music. You fell off."

ety: From Latin ratiōcinor (“to reckon, argue”) + -ate, from ratiō + -cinor. First use appears c.1643 in the writings of Kenelm Digby.

s.def: To use the powers of the mind logically and methodically; to reason.

ety: From French ration. Doublet of reason and ratio.

s.def: A portion of some limited resource, especially food, allocated to a person, group or period.
ex: Jack gathered his meager ration of food.
The town's ration of gasoline had to go to necessary vehicles.
Betty had divided up her cigarettes to last all month, and her ration for today was only three.

s.def: To supply with a ration; to limit (someone) to a specific allowance of something.
ex: We rationed ourselves to three sips of water a day until we were rescued.

s.def: To portion out (especially during a shortage of supply); to limit access to.
ex: By the third day on the raft, we had to ration our water.

s.def: To restrict (an activity etc.)
ex: I've rationed myself to one cup of coffee a day.

ety: From Old French rationel, rational, from Latin rationalis (“of or belonging to reason, rational, reasonable; having a ratio”), from ratio (“reason; calculation”).

s.def: Capable of reasoning.
ex: Man is a rational creature.
The utility of valid arguments is a monument to our frailty: to the fact that we are not completely rational beings.

s.def: Logically sound; not self-contradictory or otherwise absurd.
ex: His statements were quite rational.

s.def: Healthy or balanced intellectually; exhibiting reasonableness.
ex: rational conduct
Temperature 99.8 degrees. Pulse 104. She was quite conscious and rational at times, at others very noisy.

s.def: Comprising, or expressible as, a ratio
ex: ¾ is a rational number, but √2 is an irrational number.

s.def: synonymous replacement for "condensed" in condensed formula.
A rational number: a number that can be expressed as the quotient of two integers.
ex: The quotient of two rationals is again a rational.

s.def: The breastplate worn by Israelite high priests.
Any function expressible as the quotient of two (coprime) polynomials (and which thus has poles at a finite, discrete set of points which are the roots of the denominator).
ex: Our first problem is that of interpolation in prescribed points to a given function by a rational function whose poles are given.

ety: From rational + number, ultimately from Latin rationalis + numerus. Compare analogous logarithm, from Ancient Greek.

s.def: A number that can be expressed as the ratio of two integers.

ety: From Late Latin ratiōnāle.

s.def: An explanation of the basis or fundamental reasons for something.
A justification or rationalization for something.
A liturgical vestment worn by some Christian bishops of various denominations.
ex: the local bishop, H.E. Gregor Maria Hanke, is shown wearing that rarest of liturgical garments, the rationale.

ety: Etymology tree English rational Proto-Indo-European *-id- Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-idyéti Proto-Hellenic *-íd͏̌d͏̌ō Ancient Greek -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō) Proto-Indo-European *-mos Proto-Indo-European *-mós Ancient Greek -μός (-mós) Ancient Greek -ισμός (-ismós)der. English -ism English rationalism From rational + -ism.

s.def: The theory that reason is a source of knowledge independent of and superior to sense perception.
The theory that knowledge may be derived by deductions from a priori concepts (such as axioms, postulates or earlier deductions).
A view that the fundamental method for problem solving is through reason and experience rather than faith, inspiration, revelation, intuition or authority.
Elaboration of theories by use of reason alone without appeal to experience, such as in mathematical systems.

ety: From Middle French rationaliste; rational + -ist.

s.def: A person who follows the philosophy of rationalism.
A member of the rationalist community.

ety: From rational + -ity, from French rationalité, from Late Latin rationalitas (“rationality, reasonableness”), from Latin rationalis (“reasonable”).

s.def: The quality or state of being rational; due exercise of reason; reasonableness.
ex: His sudden loss of rationality was brought on by excess drink.

s.def: Objective consideration.
ex: Such a discussion deserves rationality, not emotional gut reactions.

ety: First attested in 1831. From French rationalisation, equivalent to rational + -ization or rationalize + -ation.

s.def: The process or result of rationalizing, or expressing in rational terms.
ex: Some rationalization of the language of his lectures is, of course, necessary.

s.def: A statement of one's motives, or of the causes of some event.
ex: Her self-flagellating rationalization for the theft was mostly ignored by the jury.

s.def: The reorganization of a company or organization in order to improve its efficiency through the reallocation of resources and changes in its workforce.
ex: It began with the familiar political motives of civil service rationalization and downsizing.

s.def: The concealment of true motivation in some non-threatening way.
The simplification of an expression without changing its value.
ex: Here, the rationalization of the denominator was unnecessary.

ety: From French rationaliser. By surface analysis, rational + -ize.

s.def: To make something rational or more rational.
To justify a discreditable act, or irrational behaviour.
ex: Vested interest, united ties, / landed gentry, rationalize. / Look who bought the myth. / By jingo, buy America.

s.def: To remove radicals, without changing the value of an expression or the roots of an equation.
To structure something along modern, efficient and systematic lines, or according to scientific principles. This often includes eliminating duplication and grouping like or similar items.

ety: From Latin ratis (“raft”) + -ite; ratites (unlike other birds) lack a keel on their sternum, and rafts are vessels that lack keels.

s.def: Pertaining to running, flightless birds with no keels on their sternums (as opposed to carinate).
ex: Against what was probably the general expectation, it became undeniable that New Zealand was indeed the home of huge ratite birds.

s.def: A member of a diverse group of mostly large, running, flightless birds that lack keels on their sternums, mostly extinct such as the elephant bird and the moa, but including the extant cassowaries, emu, kiwi, ostrich, and rhea; formerly grouped together in the order Struthioniformes, and including…

ety: Apparently a corruption of raddling by folk-etymological reanalysis as rat + line.

s.def: The rope or similar material used to make cross-ropes on a ship.
Any of the cross ropes between the shrouds, which form a net-like ropework, allowing sailors to climb up towards the top of the mast.
ex: That meant it was not possible to use ratlines — that is, to make rope ladders out of the shrouds by adding small connecting pieces of ropes.

s.def: A system of escape routes for Nazis and other fascists fleeing Europe in the aftermath of World War II.
ex: Marc Masurovsky, of the European Shoah Legacy Institute, has a remarkable knowledge of the Nazi ratlines and Allied intelligence.

ety: From rat's + bane. Compare henbane.

s.def: Rat poison; white arsenic.
ex: Before him set the grim baron, with a face worthy of the father of such a daughter, and looking daggers and rat's bane.

ety: From rat + tail: all of the nonliteral senses come from something else's fancied resemblance to the tail of a rat.

A fish, a California chimera (Hydrolagus colliei, syn. Chimaera colliei).
A hairstyle characterized by a long lock of tail-like hair dangling from the back of the head; the dangling lock itself.
A type of file (cutting tool) with a round cross section and usually also a taper toward the distal end.
A towel that has been tightly twisted along the diagonal to make a rudimentary whip with a towel corner at the tip, typically used in juvenile pranks.
An excrescence growing from the pastern to the middle of the shank of a horse.
The flowering plant Stachytarpheta cayennensis.

ety: Borrowed from Malay rotan.

s.def: Any of several species of climbing palm of the genus Calamus.
A cane made from this material.
ex: He who first acts as striker asks the other how many blows of the rattan he will bear on his forearm without crying out.
[…]the rattan is still a valued instrument of discipline[…]

s.def: The plant used as a material for making furniture, baskets etc.
ex: It took Elwood an hour to find Mr. Gladwell, who sat in a big rattan chair at the edge of the sweet potato fields.

s.def: To beat with a rattan cane.
ex: Meanwhile Captain Colville rattaned Pearson very severely […]

ety: From Middle English ratelen, of uncertain origin; perhaps borrowed from Middle Dutch ratelen or of native origin related to Old English hratele, hrætele (“a plant known for its rustling or rattling sound”), ultimately imitative. The noun (c. 1500) is from the verb.

s.def: To create a rattling sound by shaking or striking.
ex: to rattle a chain
Rattle the can of cat treats if you need to find Fluffy.

s.def: To scare, startle, unsettle, or unnerve.
To make a rattling noise; to make noise by or from shaking.
ex: I wish the dashboard in my car would quit rattling.

s.def: To assail, annoy, or stun with a rattling noise.
To scold; to rail at.
ex: This came to the Bishop's Ear, who presently sent for the Curate, Rattled him to some Tune, with Menaces to the Highest Degree

s.def: To drive or ride briskly, so as to make a clattering.
ex: We rattled along for a couple of miles.

s.def: To make a clatter with one's voice; to talk rapidly and idly; often with on or away.
ex: She rattled on for an hour.

s.def: To experience withdrawal from drugs.
Object that rattles.
ex: Pleas'd with a rattle, tickled with a straw.

s.def: Rattling sound.
ex: I wish they would fix the rattle under my dashboard.
The rattle of a drum.

ety: From rattle + box.

s.def: A toy or instrument that makes a rattle sound; a rattle.
An American herb (Crotalaria sagittalis), whose ripe seeds rattle in the inflated pod.
Any species of Crotalaria, a genus of yellow-flowered herbs, with inflated, many-seeded pods.
An ornamental shrub (Sesbania punicea) native to Brazil, Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay.
Any species of Rhinanthus, a genus of annual hemiparasitic herbaceous plants.
Senna covesii, a perennial subshrub native to the United States and Mexico.
A species of moth, (Utetheisa ornatrix), that feeds on Crotalaria.

ety: Etymology tree English rattle Proto-Germanic *sneganą Proto-Germanic *snakaną Proto-West Germanic *snakan Proto-Indo-European *-ō Proto-Germanic *-ô Proto-West Germanic *-ō Proto-West Germanic *snakō Old English snaca Middle English snake English snake English rattlesnake From rattle + snake.

s.def: Any of various venomous American snakes, of genera Crotalus and Sistrurus, having a rattle at the end of its tail.
ex: Hooded rattlesnakes, horned toads, and lizards crawl in the dust and among the rocks.

ety: From rattle + trap.

s.def: Mechanically unreliable or in disrepair.
A mechanical device, particularly an automobile, that is worn out, run down, or mechanically unreliable as indicated by noises it makes in operation.
ex: Mom always worried about our safety in my friend's rattletrap. I told her not to worry, as it can't go fast enough to be dangerous.

s.def: Any piece of miscellaneous equipment or junk.
ex: And they tumbled about the rattletraps under the cupboard, and rummaged the drawers in search of the sacred volume.

s.def: A type of noisemaker in which the teeth of a gear repeatedly bend and release a stiff tongue.
A person's mouth.
ex: Shut your rattletrap!

s.def: Lively, quick (speech, pace).
good, fine.
ex: a rattling good lunch
To say the truth, Sophia, when very young, discerned that Tom, though an idle, thoughtless, rattling rascal, was nobody's enemy but his own […]

s.def: present participle and gerund of rattle
rattle (a sound made by objects shaking or vibrating against one another)
Alternative form of ratline.

ety: From rattle + -y. Compare rattling.

s.def: That rattles.
ex: a rattly air conditioner

s.def: Resembling the sound of a rattle.
Of a vehicle, that shakes when being driven.
Of the lungs, chest, etc., producing raspy or gurgling sound due to excess mucus.

ety: From Middle English rat trappe; equivalent to rat + trap.

s.def: A device (trap) used to catch rats.
A dilapidated building, a place that is run down and unsanitary.
A difficult, entangling situation.
A type of bicycle pedal made of metal with no rubber.

ety: From rat + -y (suffix meaning ‘having the quality of’ forming adjective).

s.def: Crazy, mad; ridiculous; slightly strange, eccentric; also (followed by about, on, or over), attracted to, infatuated with.
Annoyed, bad-tempered, irritable.
ex: He got bad, he got ratty, he would take it out on people around him. He was mean when it turned against him.

s.def: Resembling or characteristic of a rat; ratlike.
Infested with rats.
In poor condition or repair.
ex: The Marcher lord was still clad in his ratty black cloak and dented breastplate with its chipped enamel lightning.
I was having exactly that thought on a ratty mock-leather couch in Islington.

s.def: Synonym of knock down ginger (“prank of knocking on a front door and running away”).

ety: Etymology tree Latin rāvis Proto-Indo-European *-kos Proto-Italic *-kos Latin -cus Latin raucusbor. English raucous Borrowed from Latin raucus (“hoarse, husky, raucous”).

s.def: Harsh and rough-sounding.
ex: At night, raucous ruckus took place in the swamp.

s.def: Disorderly and boisterous.
ex: Acts of vandalism were committed by a raucous gang of drunkards.

s.def: Loud and annoying.
ex: The new neighbors had a raucous ruction in the small hours last night.
There are also a lot of people who have never dreamed of being disagreeable in public, much less considered joining a raucous social movement.

ety: From French ravage (“ravage, havoc, spoil”), from ravir (“to bear away suddenly”), from Latin rapere (“to snatch, seize”), akin to Ancient Greek ἁρπάζω (harpázō, “to seize”).

s.def: To devastate, destroy or lay waste to something.
To pillage or plunder destructively; to sack.
To wreak destruction.
To have vigorous sexual intercourse with.
To rape.
Grievous damage or havoc.
ex: Would one think 'twere possible for love / To make such ravage in a noble soul!

s.def: Depredation or devastation.
ex: the ravages of fire or tempest
the ravages of an army
the ravages of time

ety: From Middle English raven (“to rave; talk like a madman”), from Old French raver, variant of resver, of uncertain origin. Compare rave below, and rove.

s.def: An enthusiastic review (such as of a play).
ex: It was the critic's rave that made me want to see the show.

s.def: A large-scale dance party with strobe lights and fast-paced electronic dance music, often illegally organized open-air or in underground venues.
ex: She has attended a rave every weekend this month.

s.def: The genres of electronic dance music made to be played in rave parties.
ex: I danced to rave music all night.
Maybe I wear baggies / And white socks with flip-flops / Maybe I don't like listening to rave / And I'm not on the social mountaintops

s.def: To be mentally unclear; to be delirious; to talk or act irrationally; to be wild, furious, or raging.
ex: Have I not cause to rave and beat my breast?
The mingled torrent of redcoats and tartans went raving down the valley to the gorge of Killiecrankie.

s.def: To speak or write wildly or incoherently.
ex: "She is in trance. Your daughter, sir, is a powerful medium." "A medium! You are raving."

s.def: To speak (a message) with intense enthusiasm, passion or excitement.
ex: She raved that she must seek revenge against the wrongdoers.
"Paloma, Paloma!" raved a delirious backer. "Paloma for a thousand!"
some-times she raved that she cared nought for the future happiness of Ram Ruoy and would not go.

s.def: To rush wildly or furiously.
ex: Under a mightie rocke, gainst which do rave The roaring billowes in their proud disdaine

s.def: To attend a rave (dance party).
To talk or otherwise express oneself with excessive enthusiasm, passion or excitement.
ex: He raved about her beauty.
The Lisbon mob, inflamed by the newspapers, and excited by the example of Brazil, raved a day or two for a republic
The hallowed scene / Which others rave on, though they know it not.

s.def: To wander or roam.

syn: have a kangaroo loose in the top paddock

ety: The verb is borrowed from Dutch ravelen, rafelen (“to tangle, become entangled; to fray; to unweave”) [and other forms]; further etymology uncertain. It has been suggested that the verb is originally derived from the noun, but the Oxford English Dictionary regards this as “very uncertain”, and instead regards the noun as having derived from the verb (compare Dutch rafel, raffel (“frayed thread”)). Ravel is a contranym having both the senses of tangling (verb senses 1.1, 1.2, 1.4.1, and 2.3; nou…

s.def: To entwine or tangle (something) confusedly; to entangle.
Often followed by up: to form (something) out of discrete elements, like weaving fabric from threads; to knit.

To unwind (a reel of thread, a skein of yarn, etc.); to pull apart (cloth, a seam, etc.); to fray, to unpick, to unravel; also, to pull out (a string of yarn, a thread, etc.) from a piece of fabric, or a skein or reel.
ex: If there be any fault in the verses, I can mend it extempore; for a stitch in a man's stocking not taken up in time, ravels out all the rest.

s.def: Often followed by out: to undo the intricacies of (a problem, etc.); to clarify, to disentangle.
To destroy or ruin (something), like unravelling fabric.
To confuse or perplex (someone or something).
In the APL programming language: to reshape (a variable) into a vector.
Often followed by out: of clothing, fabric, etc.: to become unwoven; to fray, to unravel.
ex: But the real work of the First Thursday Foundation is remembering, and its biggest gift is knitting back together lives raveled by loss.

s.def: To become entangled or snarled.
Often followed by out: of a reel of thread or skein of yarn; or a thread on a reel or a string of yarn in a skein, etc.: to become untwisted or unwound.

ety: From ravel + -ment.

ex: 0.5 is the reciprocal of 2.

ety: From Latin recīprocātus, perfect passive participle of recīprocō (“to move back and forth”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from reciprocus (“back an forth, reciprocal, alternating”) + -ō (first conjugation verb-forming suffix), itself possibly from a phrase such as reque proque (“back and forth”), from re- (“back”), prō (“forwards”) and -que (“and”). ety: From Middle English redolent (first attested in 1400), from Old French redolent, from Latin redolentem, present participle of redoleō (“to emit a scent”), from red- + oleō (“to smell”).

The return of doubt.

To put in order again; to set right; to revise.

To put upright again; to restore.
The act of redressing; a making right; amendment; correction; reformation.
A setting right, as of injury, oppression, or wrong, such as the redress of grievances; hence, indemnification; relief; remedy; reparation.

ety: Inherited from Middle English *redstert; equivalent to red + start (“tail”). Compare Dutch roodstaart, Danish rødstjert.

ety: From red + stone, after its color.

ety: From Middle English reducen, from Old French reduire, from Latin redūcō (“reduce”); from re- (“back”) + dūcō (“lead”). See duke, and compare with redoubt.

s.def: To add electrons / hydrogen or to remove oxygen.
ex: Formaldehyde can be reduced to form methanol.

ex: to reduce weight, speed, heat, expenses, price, personnel etc.

ety: From Middle English reduccion, a borrowing from Old French reducion, from Latin reductiō, reductiōnem. Equivalent to reduce + -tion.

The amount or rate by which something is reduced, e.g. in price.
ex: A 5% reduction in robberies

The rewriting of an expression into a simpler form.
A transformation of one problem into another problem, such as mapping reduction or polynomial-time reduction.
An arrangement for a far smaller number of parties, e.g. a keyboard solo based on a full opera.
A philosophical procedure intended to reveal the objects of consciousness as pure phenomena. (See phenomenological reduction.)
A medical procedure to restore a fracture or dislocation to the correct alignment, usually with a closed approach but sometimes with an open approach (surgery).

open reduction and internal fixation

ety: From Middle English rek, reke (“smoke”), from Old English rēc, from Proto-West Germanic *rauki, from Proto-Germanic *raukiz, from Proto-Indo-European *rowgi-. Cognate with West Frisian reek, riik, Dutch rook (“smoke”), Low German Röök, German Rauch (“smoke”), Danish røg (“smoke”), Norwegian Bokmål and Norwegian Nynorsk røyk (“smoke”), Swedish rök (“smoke”), Faroese roykur (“smoke”), Icelandic reykur (“smoke”); also Lithuanian rū̃kti (“to smoke”), rū̃kas (“smoke, fog”), Albanian regj (“to tan”).

ety: From Middle English [Term?], from past participle of Old French referer (“to relate, to refer”), from Latin referre (“to carry back, to report, to notify”); as if refer + -ee, that is, the person to whom something is referred for consideration.

A person who writes a letter of reference or provides a reference by phone call for someone. (In the UK such a person is sometimes, and in the US the person is typically, referred to as a reference.)
ex: Your application, along with letters from three referees, should be received by January 31.

ety: From Middle French référence, from Medieval Latin referentia, nominative neuter plural of referēns, present participle of referō (“return, reply”, literally “carry back”). Morphologically refer + -ence.

A short written identification of a previously published work which is used as a source for a text.
An object containing information which refers to data stored elsewhere, as opposed to containing the data itself.

ety: From Latin referendum (“that which ought to be announced”), from refero (“to announce”).

ex: My father is taking my decision on whether to go to university as a referendum on his performance as a parent, and it's very stressful.

ety: From refer + -er.

a refined style

to refine someone's language

s.def: Dealing in a refined product such as sugar or petroleum.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- English fine English refine Middle English -re, -ri, -rie, -ry, -rye English -ry English refinery From refine + -ry.

s.def: A building, or a mass of machinery, used to produce refined products such as sugar, oil, or metals.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- Middle English fit? English fit English refit From re- + fit.

s.def: The process of having something fitted again, repaired or restored.

To prepare a vessel for use again (e.g. by replenishing depleted supplies or doing maintenance or repair work); (of a vessel) to be prepared for use again.
ex: As soon as we were out of danger, we came to anchor and refitted;

ety: From Old French reflecter (“to bend back, turn back”), from Latin reflectō (“to reflect”), from re- (“again”) + flectō (“to bend, to curve”). Compare English reflex.

ex: A mirror reflects the light that shines on it.

ex: The moonlight reflected from the surface of water.

ex: The shop window reflected his image as he walked past.

ex: His image reflected from the shop window as he walked past.

ex: The team's victory reflects the Captain's abilities.

ex: Entries in English dictionaries aim to reflect common usage.

s.def: To think seriously; to ponder or consider.
ex: People do that sort of thing every day, without ever stopping to reflect on the consequences.

An instance of reflection (in any sense).
That has been reflected (of light, sound etc.); undergoing reflection.
That reflects.

s.def: Having a component that reflects light.

s.def: Given to introspection; thoughtful, reflective.
Insulting, disparaging.

ety: From Middle English refleccion, refleccioun, refleccioune, reflection, from Middle French reflection, reflexion, and its source Late Latin reflexiō, from the participle stem of reflectō. The current spelling is influenced by reflect. Equivalent to reflect + -ion.

Something, such as an image, that is reflected.

s.def: The folding of a part; a fold.

ex: to refund a railroad loan

s.def: To pour back (something).
ex: Were the humours of the eye tinctured with any colour, they would refund that colour upon the object.

s.def: An amount of money returned.
ex: If the camera is faulty, you can return it to the store where you bought it for a full refund.

ety: Inherited from Middle English refusell. By surface analysis, refuse + -al.

s.def: The act of refusing.
ex: Your refusal to carry out your duties resulted in your sacking.

s.def: Depth or point at which well or borehole drilling cannot continue.

ety: Borrowed into late Middle English from Middle French refusé, past participle of refuser (“to refuse”). Displaced native Middle English wernen (“to refuse”) likely due to the similar sounding Middle English warnen

s.def: Discarded, rejected.
Collectively, items or material that have been discarded; rubbish, garbage.
(transitive) decline (request, demand)
To decline (a request or demand).
ex: My request for a pay rise was refused.

s.def: To decline a request or demand, forbear; to withhold permission.
ex: I refuse to listen to this nonsense any more.
I asked the star if I could have her autograph, but she refused.
If ye refuse […] ye shall be devoured with the sword.

s.def: To withhold (something) from (someone); to not give it to them or to bar them from having it.
To throw back, or cause to keep back (as the centre, a wing, or a flank), out of the regular alignment when troops are about to engage the enemy.
ex: to refuse the right wing while the left wing attacks

s.def: To disown.
refusal
To fuse again, as with, or after, heating or melting.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French refutation (compare French réfutation, Spanish refutación, Portuguese refutação, Italian refutazione) or its etymon Latin refūtātiō, from refūtō + -ātiō. By surface analysis, refute + -ation. First attested in 1536 (in sense 1).

s.def: An act of refuting or disproving; the disproving of an argument, opinion, testimony, doctrine or theory by argument or countervailing proof; evidence of falseness.
ex: Near-synonyms: rebuttal (see note), counterargument, counterassertion, counterclaim, denial

s.def: A vocal answer to an attack on one's assertions.

ety: From Latin refūtō (“refute, repudiate”).

s.def: To prove (something) to be false or incorrect.
To deny the truth or correctness of (something); to reject or disagree with an accusation.
ex: A spokesperson for VARS Technology said: “We completely refute the suggestion that our market-leading ANPR system is unreliable".

ety: From Middle French regaigner (French regagner). By surface analysis, re- + gain.

s.def: To get back; to recover possession of.
The act or process of regaining something.
ex: The samples with SAPs showed a regain in strength when stored in an RH of more than 90%.
Negative collective memories are effective, as much as positive memories, in choosing a regain for lost heritage building associated with them.

s.def: The amount of width a woven cloth grows by when the fibers swell, used to determine the width of the reed to use in weaving.
ex: In particular, at high humidities the regain of wool is lower.
Because of the fiber price per pound, and the size of the lots, the regain must be determined accurately.

ety: From Middle English regal, from Old French regal (“regal, royal”), from Latin rēgālis (“royal, kingly”), from rex (“king”); also regere (“to rule”). Doublet of royal (“belonging to a monarch”), real (“unit of currency”), ariary, and riyal. Cognate with Spanish real, Italian reale, Catalan reial.

s.def: Of, pertaining to, or suitable for royalty.
ex: regal authority
the regal title
He made a scorn of his regal oath.

s.def: Befitting a monarch.
ex: Terrific movement from The Queen here. Gets behind the defender, goes one way then cuts back inside. Regal attacking play.
Kwarteng said he had urged Truss to “slow down” over reforms, but a cabinet minister told the FT that she felt “invincible, almost regal”.

s.def: A small, portable organ whose sound is produced by brass beating reeds without amplifying resonators. Its tone is keen and rich in harmonics. The regal was common in the 16th and 17th centuries, and has been revived for the performance of music from those times.

An organ stop of the reed family, furnished with a normal beating reed, but whose resonator is a fraction of its natural length. In the 16th and 17th centuries these stops took a multitude of forms. Today only one survives that is of universal currency, the so-called vox humana.

ety: From French régaler (“to entertain, feast”), from Old French regale, rigale, from gale (“merriment”), probably of Germanic origin (see Old French galer). Influenced by Old French se rigoler (“amuse oneself, rejoice”), of unknown origin. Compare Middle High German begalen (“to charm; enchant”), English gale (“to sing; charm”). Compare also English gala.

s.def: A feast, a meal.
a choice article of food or drink.
refreshment.
To provide hospitality for (someone); to supply with abundant food and drink.
To please or entertain (someone), especially with stories, tales or jokes.
ex: Please, regale us with your best tales!

s.def: To feast (on, with something).
ex: she hardly lets a Week pass without making the Lady Abbess and her Nuns a Visit, to regale with a Cup of burnt Brandy.

s.def: To entertain with something that delights; to gratify; to refresh.
ex: to regale the taste/the eye/the ear

ety: From Middle English regalie, from Medieval Latin rēgālia (“royal powers”), substantivisation of the neuter plural of rēgālis (“of a king”), from rēx (“king”). By surface analysis, regal + -ia.

s.def: Royal rights, prerogatives and privileges actually enjoyed by any sovereign, regardless of his title (emperor, grand duke etc.).
The emblems, symbols, or paraphernalia indicative of royalty or any other sovereign status; such as a crown, orb, sceptre or sword.
Decorations or insignia indicative of an office or membership of an order or society; such as freemasonry.
Traditional dress and accessories of North American Indigenous nations worn for ritual purposes.
Finery, magnificent dress, or lavish or flashy costume.
ex: to be dressed in full regalia (dressed up)

s.def: Sumptuous food.
A kind of large cigar of superior quality.
ex: I have taken care that there's both brandy and whiskey nicely stowed away in the barrack-room, with plenty of prime regalia cigars[…]
The quantity of regalias imported into northern ports is comparatively small.

ety: From Middle English regalite, from Old French, from Late Latin rēgālitās, from Latin rēgālis (“regal, royal”), equivalent to regal + -ity. Doublet of royalty.

s.def: Royalty; sovereignty; sovereign jurisdiction.

ety: From Middle English regard, regarde, reguard, from Anglo-Norman reguard, from regarder, reguarder. Attested in Middle English starting around the mid 14th century. Piecewise doublet of reward; compare also guard, ward, guardian, and so on.

s.def: A steady look, a gaze.
One's concern for another; esteem; relation, reference.
A particular aspect or detail; respect, sense.
ex: This attempt will be made with every regard to the difficulty of the undertaking […]
We are spending a lot of money trying to put this mine in shape; we are anxious to comply with the wishes of your office in every regard […]
These problems were not traditional problems with realistic stimuli, but rather were realistic in every regard.

s.def: The worth or estimation in which something or someone is held.
ex: He is held in great regard in Whitehall.

s.def: To look at; to observe.
ex: She regarded us warily.

s.def: To consider, look upon (something) in a given way etc.
ex: I always regarded tabloid journalism as a social evil.
He regards honesty as a duty, but was regarded himself as (being) rather dangerous by the police.
She regarded her pets as an extension of the family.

s.def: To take notice of, pay attention to.
To face toward.
To have to do with, to concern.
ex: That argument does not regard the question.

s.def: To set store by (something), to hold (someone) in esteem; to consider to have value, to respect.
ex: Ther was a Iudge in a certayne cite which feared not god nether regarded man.

ety: From regard + -ful.

s.def: Respectful.
Watchful, observant.

ety: By surface analysis, regard + -ing.

s.def: present participle and gerund of regard
Concerning, respecting.
The act by which something is regarded or observed.
ex: […] God Invisible by the assumption of His Manhood was laid open to the regardings of our sight.

ety: Etymology tree English regard Proto-Indo-European *lewh₁- Proto-Indo-European *lewHs-der. Proto-Germanic *leusaną Proto-Germanic *lausaz Proto-Germanic *-lausaz Proto-West Germanic *-laus Old English -lēas Middle English -les English -less English regardless From regard + -less.

s.def: Without attention to warnings or indications of bad consequences.
ex: Tatiana knew the meat had passed its expiry date, but she ate it regardless.

s.def: Anyway; irrespective of what has just been said.
ex: The proposal may become law, or it may not. Regardless, we will adopt it as a club rule.

s.def: Paying no attention to; ignoring.
ex: The beloved “oof” sound Roblox players — and gamers regardless of what they play — has become a huge meme in the community.

s.def: Taking insufficient regard of; heedless; careless.
ex: Always deceived in fact by his own wishes, and regardless of little besides his own convenience.
I grew, day by day, more moody, more irritable, more regardless of the feelings of others.

s.def: Synonym of regardless of; paying no attention to.
ex: Tatiana ate the cauliflower regardless its colour.

ety: From Italian (Venetian dialect) regatta (“contention for mastery”), from regattare (“compete, haggle, sell at retail”), possibly from ricattare; or from Italian regata (“boat race, regatta”), via Vulgar Latin *aurigata from Latin auriga.

s.def: A series of boat races, or sometimes a single race.
A striped cotton fabric.
A group of swans on the water.
ex: As he quietly planned out the unfolding day ahead of him, his attention was drawn to a regatta of swans drawing close to the bank of the river.

ety: From Middle English regencie (cf. regente), from Medieval Latin regentia, from Latin regēns, present participle of regō. By surface analysis, regent + -cy; compare also + -ency (“abstract-noun suffix”).

s.def: A system of government that substitutes for the reign of a king or queen when that king or queen becomes unable to rule.
The time during which a regent is in power.
An administrative division ranking below a province in Indonesia.

ety: From Latin regenerātus, perfect passive participle of regenerō, from re- + generō, from genus, generis (“descent, origin, birth”); -ō, equivalent to re- + generate.

s.def: To construct or create anew, especially in an improved manner.
To revitalize.
To replace lost or damaged tissue.
To become reconstructed.
To undergo a spiritual rebirth.
Of a water softener: to flush out the minerals extracted from the water supply.
Spiritually reborn.
Reproduced.
One who is spiritually reborn.

ety: From regenerate + -er.

s.def: One who, or that which, regenerates.
ex: regenerator of content

s.def: A type of heat exchanger where heat from the hot fluid is intermittently stored in a thermal storage medium before it is transferred to the cold fluid.

ety: From Middle English regent, from Anglo-Norman regent, Middle French regent, and their source, Latin regēns (“ruling; ruler, governor, prince”), present participle of regō (“to govern, to steer”).

s.def: One who rules in place of the monarch, especially because the monarch is too young, absent, or disabled.
Any ruler.
A member of a municipal or civic body of governors, especially in certain European cities.
ex: This perception, however, does no justice to the regents of the city of Amsterdam.

s.def: A member of governing board of a college or university; also a governor of the Smithsonian Institution in Washington, D.C.
The chief executive of a regency.
Exercising vicarious authority.
ex: the regent powers

s.def: Ruling; governing; regnant.
ex: Some other active regent principle […] which we call the soul.

ety: From Jamaican Creole rege (“rags; a quarrel”), see rag; originally used in the 1960s to describe a Jamaican dance. Compare ragtime. Broader musical sense popularized by the 1968 Maytals song “Do the Reggay”.

s.def: A music genre that originated in Jamaica in the late 1960s and is heavily associated with Rastafarianism, featuring a heavy bass line and percussive rhythm guitar on the offbeat, often with close vocal harmonies.
ex: Near-synonym: (earlier) bluebeat
I want to do the reggay with you / Come onto me, do the dance

ety: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin rēgicidium (“king-killing”)

s.def: The killing of a king.
One who kills a king.
A government monopoly, such as on tobacco, typically used to raise revenue (via taxes).
ex: What is a regie government? Mr. BARKER. Where the government owns the tobacco absolutely, puts the price on it and sells it.

ety: From Middle English regime, regyme, from Middle French regime, from Latin regimen (“direction, government”). Doublet of regimen.

s.def: A form of government, or the government in power, particularly an authoritarian or totalitarian one.
ex: the dictator's regime
Heaven will eliminate the tyrannical regimes.

s.def: Mode of rule or management.
ex: a prison regime

s.def: A period of rule.
A regulated system; a regimen.
ex: a fitness regime
For three weeks Lorde engages in a regime of rest, relaxation, eurhythmy, and active meditation.

s.def: A division of a Mafia crime family, led by a caporegime.
A set of characteristics.
ex: A typical annual water level regime would include a gradual summer drawdown beginning in early May.

ety: From Middle English regimen, from Middle French regimen and its etymon, Latin regimen (“guidance, direction, government, rule”). Doublet of regime.

s.def: Orderly government; system of order; administration.
ex: In ski areas like Arapahoe Basin, about 80 percent of the male patrollers have had to drastically change (or introduce) shaving regimens.

s.def: Any regulation or remedy which is intended to produce beneficial effects by gradual operation.
ex: Seven or eight annual bloodings, and as many purgations — such was the common regimen the theory prescribed to ensure continuance of health[…]

s.def: Object.
ex: Pronouns may be nominatives, and of the direct or indirect regimen.

s.def: A syntactical relation between words, as when one depends on another and is regulated by it in respect to case or mood; government.
Diet; limitations on the food that one eats, for health reasons.

ety: From Middle French regement, régiment, and its source, Late Latin regimentum (“direction for government; course of medical treatment”), from Latin regō (“rule”).

s.def: A unit of armed troops under the command of an officer, and consisting of several smaller units.
ex: It was an old, withered man, who had served the Government in the days of the Mutiny as a native officer in a newly raised cavalry regiment.

s.def: Rule or governance over a person, place etc.; government, authority.
The state or office of a ruler; rulership.
Influence or control exercised by someone or something (especially a planet).
A place under a particular rule; a kingdom or domain.
A regimen.
To form soldiers into a regiment.
ex: The people are organized or regimented into bodies, and special functions are relegated to the several units.

s.def: To systematize, or put in rigid order.
ex: The result was a tidy, law-abiding country, but one that visitors often described as regimented, sterile and dull.

ety: Etymology tree English regiment Proto-Indo-European *-tis Proto-Indo-European *-Hō Proto-Indo-European *-tiHō Proto-Italic *-tiō Latin -tiō Latin -ātiōlbor. Old French -ationbor. Middle English -acioun English -ation English regimentation From regiment + -ation.

s.def: The act of regimenting.
ex: David hated the haircuts, the regimentation, the power plays and the "macho-male, heterosexual shop talk" of the military.

ety: From Middle English regioun, from Anglo-Norman regiun, from Latin regiō, from regō. Doublet of regio.

s.def: Any considerable and connected part of a space or surface; specifically, a tract of land or sea of considerable but indefinite extent; a country; a district; in a broad sense, a place without special reference to location or extent but viewed as an entity for geographical, social or cultural reason…
ex: the equatorial regions
the temperate regions
the polar regions

s.def: An administrative subdivision of a city, a territory, a country.
The inhabitants of a region or district of a country.
A place in or a part of the body in any way indicated.
ex: the abdominal regions

s.def: An approximate range.
ex: The average age of the club's members is in the region of 35.

s.def: Place; rank; station; dignity.
ex: he is of too high a region

s.def: The space from the earth's surface out to the orbit of the moon: properly called the elemental region.

ety: From Middle French régional, from Latin regiōnālis.

s.def: Of, or pertaining to, a specific region or district.
ex: Near-synonyms: intraregional, locoregional
regional playoffs

s.def: Of, or pertaining to, a large geographic region.
ex: regional rainfall patterns
regional language variation

s.def: Of, or pertaining to, one part of the body.
ex: Near-synonym: locoregional
regional nerve block
regional symptoms

s.def: Of a state or other geographic area, denoting those parts that are not metropolitan but are somewhat densely populated and usually contain a number of significant towns.
An entity or event with scope limited to a single region.

ety: Etymology tree English regional Proto-Indo-European *-id- Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-idyéti Proto-Hellenic *-íd͏̌d͏̌ō Ancient Greek -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō) Proto-Indo-European *-mos Proto-Indo-European *-mós Ancient Greek -μός (-mós) Ancient Greek -ισμός (-ismós)der. English -ism English regionalism From regional + -ism.

s.def: Affection, often excessive, for one's own region and to everything related to it.
The belief that most or nearly all political power should be decentralized to regional governments.
A word or phrase originating in, characteristic of, or limited to a region.
Regional character, local color.

ety: From Medieval Latin registrum, from Late Latin regesta (“list, items recorded”), from Latin regerō (“to record, to carry back”), from re- + gerō (“to carry, bear”). Compare Latin registoria (“a treasurer”). Some senses influenced by association with unrelated Latin regō (“to rule”).

s.def: To enter in a register; to enlist.
A formal recording of names, events, transactions, etc.
ex: The teacher took the register by calling out each child's name.

s.def: A book of such entries.
ex: As you have one eye upon my follies, […] turn another into the register of your own.

s.def: An entry in such a book.
The act of registering.

A certificate issued by the collector of customs of a port or district to the owner of a vessel, containing the description of a vessel, its name, ownership, and other material facts. It is kept on board the vessel, to be used as evidence of nationality or as a muniment of title.
One who registers or records; a registrar; especially, a public officer charged with the duty of recording certain transactions or events.
ex: a register of deeds

s.def: A distinct horizontal (or, more rarely, vertical) section of a work of art or inscription that is divided into several such sections.
ex: The east wall is decorated in raised relief with two registers of scenes above a dado showing a northward fecundity figure procession.

s.def: A device that automatically records a quantity.
The part of a telegraphic apparatus that automatically records the message received.
Having had one's (or its) name or identity added to an official list or entered into a register.
ex: Near-synonyms: listed, scheduled
a registered nurse
a registered voter

s.def: simple past and past participle of register

ety: From Medieval Latin registrārius, from registrum (“register”) + -ārius (“agent of use”). See more at register. By surface analysis, register /registry (“a record”) + -ar.

s.def: An official keeper or recorder of records.
A doctor receiving advanced specialist training in some countries in order to become a consultant.
A service that manages the reservation of domain names.

ety: Etymology tree English register Proto-Indo-European *-tis Proto-Indo-European *-Hō Proto-Indo-European *-tiHō Proto-Italic *-tiō Latin -tiō Latin -ātiōlbor. Old French -ationbor. Middle English -acioun English -ation English registration From register + -ation.

s.def: The act of signing up or registering for something.
ex: Complete the registration process.

s.def: That which registers or makes something official, e.g. the form or paper that registers.
ex: Did you submit your car registration yet?

s.def: Alignment, e.g. of colors or other elements in a printing process.
The location where guests register, especially with a hotel.
ex: The elevators are just past registration.

s.def: The art of selecting and combining the stops or registers of an organ.
Ellipsis of registration number.
ex: Did you get their registration?

s.def: Series of letters and numbers on shown on the front and back of a motor vehicle.

ety: A variant of registery, from Middle English regestery (“?a record book; ?a bookmark”), partly from Medieval Latin regesterium, registerium and probably also partly formed with -ery. Equivalent to register + -y.

s.def: A building in which things are registered or where registers are kept.
A database of configuration settings etc. maintained by the Microsoft Windows operating system.
ex: To unregister a DLL and remove the corresponding entries from the registry, add the /u switch to the command […]

s.def: A record; an account; a register.
The act of registering; registration.

ety: From Middle English regnant, reignant, from Middle French regnant, régnant, and its source, Latin rēgnāns, the present participle of regnāre.

s.def: Dominant; holding sway; having particular power or influence.
ex: The doors of his temples were kept open in time of war, the time in which the ideas of contradiction and conflict are most naturally regnant.

s.def: Reigning, ruling; currently holding power.
of a monarch, ruling in one's own right; often contrasted with consort and dowager
ex: Queen Elizabeth II reigned as queen regnant, unlike her mother Queen Elizabeth The Queen Mother.

s.def: A sovereign or ruler.

ety: From French regorger. Compare regurgitate.

s.def: To disgorge or vomit.
ex: it was scoffingly said that he had eaten the kings goose and did then regorge the feathers

s.def: To swallow again; to swallow back.
ex: Tides at highest mark regorge the flood.

ety: French regratter (“to scrape again”).

s.def: to grate again
ex: The Parmesan cheese needs to be regrated into smaller bits.

s.def: To purchase goods from a market in order to resell them at the same (or nearby) market at an inflated price.
To remove the outer surface of, as of an old hewn stone, so as to give it a fresh appearance.
To offend; to shock.
ex: whose clothing may regrate the eye

ety: (verb) From Latin regressus, past participle of regredior (“to go back”), from re- (“back”) + gradior (“to go”). Doublet of regressus.

s.def: The act of passing back; passage back; return; retrogression.
ex: The key-hole was still their port of egress and regress, and it resembled the aperture of a bee-hive, on a sunny day in June.
Its bearing on the progress or regress of man is not an inconsiderable question.

s.def: The power or liberty of passing back.
The right of a person (such as a lessee) to return to a property.
To move backwards to an earlier stage; to devolve.
ex: Your nightmares stopped when you were eight years old, but after the house burned down, you regressed.

s.def: To move in the retrograde direction.
To reduce in severity or size (as of a tumor), without reaching total remission.
To perform a regression on an explanatory variable.
ex: When we regress Y on X, we use the values of variable X to predict those of Y.

s.def: To interrogate a person in a state of trance about forgotten elements of their past.

ety: Learned borrowing from Latin regressio. Equivalent to regress + -ion. The statistics sense comes from regression to the mean.

s.def: An action of regressing, a return to a previous state.
ex: Few of these groups or communities that are classed as "savage" show no traces of regression from a more advanced cultural stage.

s.def: An action of travelling mentally back in time.
The diminishing of a cellular mass like a tumor, or of an organ size.
A psychotherapeutic method whereby healing is facilitated by inducing the patient to act out behaviour typical of an earlier developmental stage.
An analytic method to measure the association of one or more independent variables with a dependent variable.
An equation using specified and associated data for two or more variables such that one variable can be estimated from the remaining variable(s).
The reappearance of a bug in a piece of software that had previously been fixed.
The making an exercise less straining to perform by manipulating the details of its performance like loaded weight, range of motion, angle, speed.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re- Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰreh₁d-der. Proto-Germanic *grētaną Frankish *grātander. Old French *greter Old French regreterbor. Middle English regretten English regret From Middle English regretten, regreten, from Old French regreter, regrater (“to lament”), from re- (intensive prefix) + *greter, *grater (“to weep”), from Frankish *grātan (“to weep, mourn, lament”), from Proto-Germanic *grētaną (“to weep”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰreh…

s.def: feel sorry about some past thing
To feel sorry about (a thing that has or has not happened), afterthink: to wish that a thing had not happened, that something else had happened instead.
ex: He regretted his words.
I don't regret enrolling in law, but I regret not studying some Chinese.
Dear humanity, we regret bein' alien bastards, we regret comin' to Earth, and we most definitely regret the Corps just blew up our raggedy-ass fleet!

s.def: To feel sorry about (any thing).
ex: I regret that I have to do this, but I don't have a choice.
They said they regretted to inform us that the train would be late.

s.def: To miss; to feel the loss or absence of; to mourn.
ex: He more than ever regretted his home, and with increased desire longed to see his family.

s.def: Emotional pain on account of something done or experienced in the past, with a wish that it had been different; a looking back with dissatisfaction or with longing.
ex: What man does not remember with regret the first time he read Robinson Crusoe?
Never any prince expressed a more lively regret for the loss of a servant.
From its peaceful bosom [the grave] spring none but fond regrets and tender recollections.

s.def: Dislike; aversion.
ex: Is it a vertue to have some ineffective regrets to damnation, and such a Vertue too, as shall serve to ballance all our vices?

s.def: The amount of avoidable loss that results from choosing the wrong action.
ex: Under squared errorloss we show that there exists unique minimax regret solution for the problem of selecting the threshold.

s.def: One who was invited to an event who was unable to attend, but notified the organizer of this beforehand; a nonattendee.

ety: From Middle English reguler, from Anglo-Norman reguler, Middle French reguler, regulier, and their source, Latin rēgulāris (“continuing rules for guidance”), from rēgula (“rule”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reǵ- (“move in a straight line”).

s.def: Having a constant pattern; showing evenness of form or appearance.
Of a verb, plural, etc., following a set or common pattern; according to the general rules of a given language.
ex: "Walked" is the past tense of the regular verb "to walk".

s.def: Having the expected characteristics or appearances; normal, ordinary, standard.
Bound by religious rule; belonging to a monastic or religious order (often as opposed to secular).
ex: regular clergy, in distinction from the secular clergy
A quarter of a million strong in 1680, the clergy was only half as large in 1789. The unpopular regular clergy were the worst affected.

s.def: Demonstrating a consistent set of rules; showing order, evenness of operation or occurrence.
ex: April may be the cruellest month, but I am planning to render it civilised and to take my antibiotics in a regular manner.

s.def: Of a moon or other satellite: following a relatively close and prograde orbit with little inclination or eccentricity.
Well-behaved, orderly; restrained (of a lifestyle etc.).
Happening at constant (especially short) intervals.
ex: He made regular visits to go see his mother.

s.def: Both equilateral and equiangular; having all sides of the same length, and all (corresponding) angles of the same size
Permanently organised; being part of a set professional body of troops.
A concise description of a regular formal language with notations for concatenation, alternation, and iteration (repetition) of subexpressions.
Any pattern for text matching or searching, frequently offering more or less functionality than a theoretical regular expression.
A verb which conjugates regularly. In English, a verb which uses an -ed suffix to form its past participle.

ety: Etymology tree English regular Proto-Indo-European *-id- Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-idyéti Proto-Hellenic *-íd͏̌d͏̌ō Ancient Greek -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō)bor. Late Latin -izōder. Middle French -iserbor. Middle English -isen English -ize English regularize From regular + -ize.

s.def: To make regular.
ex: Regularizing spelling was an important step in the advancement of literary society.

ety: Borrowed from Latin regulatus, perfect passive participle of regulō (“to direct, rule, regulate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from regula (“rule”), from regō (“to keep straight, direct, govern, rule”). Compare regle, rail. Displaced native Old English metegian.

s.def: To adjust (a mechanism) for accurate and proper functioning.
ex: to regulate a watch, i.e. adjust its rate of running so that it will keep approximately standard time
to regulate the temperature of a room, the pressure of steam, the speed of a machine, etc.

s.def: To dictate policy.
To control or direct according to rule, principle, or law.
ex: the laws which regulate the succession of the seasons
The herdsmen near the frontier adjudicated their own disputes, and regulated their own police.

s.def: To put or maintain in order.
ex: to regulate the disordered state of a nation or its finances
to regulate one's eating habits

ety: From regulate + -ion.

s.def: The act of regulating or the condition of being regulated.
A law or administrative rule, issued by an organization, used to guide or prescribe the conduct of members of that organization.
ex: Army regulations state a soldier AWOL over 30 days is a deserter.

s.def: A type of law made by the executive branch of a government, usually as authorized by a statute made by the legislative branch giving the executive the authority to do so.
A form of legislative act which is self-effecting, and requires no further intervention by the Member States to become law.
Mechanism controlling DNA transcription.
Physiological process which consists in maintaining homoeostasis.

ety: From regulate + -or.

s.def: A device that controls or limits something.
ex: The regulator stopped working and the resulting overvoltage destroyed the device.

s.def: A person or group that sets standards of practice, especially regulatory law as sanctioned by statutory law.
ex: […]in part because a key county reservoir had to been^([sic]) drained to reduce earthquake risks highlighted by federal regulators.

s.def: A very accurate clock, used by clockmakers to measure the timekeeping of each newly made clock.
A gene involved in controlling the expression of one or more other genes.
A device that controls the supply of steam to the cylinders of a steam locomotive.
Synonym of bulldozer (“member of intimidating group of white US Southerners”).
A positive real number determining the density of the units in Dirichlet's unit theorem.
Short for diving regulator.

ety: Borrowed from Latin regulus.

s.def: An impure metal formed beneath slag during the smelting of ores.

ety: From Late Latin regurgitātus, past participle of regurgitāre, combined form of re- (“back”) + gurgitāre (“to engulf, flood”), from gurges (“whirlpool, gulf, sea, abyss”).

s.def: To throw up or vomit; to eject what has previously been swallowed.
To cough up from the gut to feed its young, as an animal or bird does.
ex: The young gulls were fed by their mother’s regurgitated food.

s.def: To repeat (information) verbatim or by rote, typically after learning it without actual comprehension.
To be thrown or poured back; to rush or surge back.
ex: Food may regurgitate from the stomach into the mouth.

s.def: Something regurgitated; regurgitated matter.

syn: bow down before the porcelain god

ety: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin rehabilitātus, perfect passive participle of Latin rehabilitō. See habilitate.

s.def: To return (someone) to good health after illness, addiction, etc.
To restore (someone) to their former state, reputation, possessions, status etc.
To vindicate; to restore the reputation or image of (a person, concept etc.).
To return (something) to its original condition.
To restore or repair (a vehicle, building); to make habitable or usable again.
To restore to (a criminal etc.) the necessary training and education to allow for a successful reintegration into society; to retrain.
To go through such a process; to recover.

ety: From Middle French réhabilitation, from Medieval Latin rehabilitatio.

s.def: The process of rehabilitating somebody or something.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- English hash English rehash From re- + hash.

s.def: To hash (chop food into small pieces) again.
ex: I never did care for Sunday joint that was served up cold on Monday, hashed on Tuesday, rissoled on Wednesday, and re-hashed on Thursday[.]

s.def: To repeat with minor variation.
ex: Today's parliamentary session only rehashed last week's arguments.
The CEO of the company only rehashed a speech for the news conference.
The general rehashed plans for the war.

s.def: To analyze a prior contentious or embarrassing event.
ex: Let's not rehash what we did last night.

s.def: To recompute the structure of a hash table, taking into account any newly added items.
Something reworked, or made up from old materials.
ex: He wrote a bad rehash of an earlier essay.

s.def: A recomputation of the structure of a hash table, taking into account any newly added items.

ety: From Middle English rehercel, rehersail, rehersall, from rehersen and apparently partly Middle French rehercel. By surface analysis, rehearse + -al.

s.def: The practising of something which is to be performed before an audience, usually to test or improve the interaction between several participating people, or to allow technical adjustments with respect to staging to be done.
A preparatory activity analogous to a rehearsal (sense 1).
ex: The forest fires are just a rehearsal for the devastation that will be caused if climate change continues to worsen.

s.def: The act of rehearsing or contriving something; the fact of something's being rehearsed.
ex: The prosecution argued that the defendant's exact repetition of his account of the events several times demonstrated the rehearsal of his story.

ety: From Middle English rehersen, from Anglo-Norman reherser (“to repeat word-for-word”).

s.def: To repeat, as what has been already said; to tell over again; to recite.
ex: There’s no need to rehearse the same old argument; we’ve heard it before, and we all agree.

s.def: To narrate; to relate; to tell; to recount.
ex: The witness rehearsed the events of the night before for the listening detectives.

s.def: To practise by recitation or repetition in private for experiment and improvement, prior to a public representation, especially in theater.
ex: The main actors spent on average two hours a day rehearsing before the first night.
The lawyer advised her client to rehearse her testimony before the trial date.

s.def: To cause to rehearse; to instruct by rehearsal.
ex: The director rehearsed the cast incessantly in the days leading up to opening night, and as a result they were tired and cranky when it arrived.
He […] has been rehearsed by Madame Defarge as to his having seen Her […]
It was plain that he'd been rehearsed a lot, but he wasn't letter-perfect by any manner of means.

s.def: To contrive and carefully prepare (a story, etc.) to offer consistency.
ex: The Crown argued that the accused had rehearsed her story.

ety: Borrowed from German Reich (“empire, realm”). Doublet of Raj.

s.def: A German empire, kingdom or nation; its territory or government.
The Third Reich; Nazi Germany.
Any empire, especially one that is imperialist, tyrannical, and/or racist.
ex: […] we are presenting our analysis of the place and significance of the remote war technology within the American Reich.
The Human Reich over nature is inherently flawed, catastrophically overextended, and soon to fall on its own sword.
The Human Reich is a fundamentally flawed bit of imagination that can never be realized, as we critically depend on an intact ecology.

ety: First attested around 1846; a macaronic calque of German Verdinglichung, using -ification (“making”) for ver- + -lich + -ung, and Latin rēs (“thing”) for Ding (“thing”)

s.def: The consideration of a human being as an impersonal object.
A process that makes a computable/addressable object out of a non-computable/addressable one; or a concrete class out of a generic one.
The transformation of a natural-language statement into a form in which its actions and events are quantifiable variables.

ety: Back-formation from reification, calque from German. Formed as Latin rēs (“thing”) + -ify (English suffix).

s.def: To regard something abstract as if it were a concrete material thing.

s.def: The exercise of sovereign power.
ex: England prospered under Elizabeth I's reign.
Throughout history, no single dictator has successfully upheld their reign forever, no matter how powerful they seemed to be.

s.def: The period during which a monarch rules.
ex: The reign of Victoria was a long one.

s.def: The territory or sphere over which a kingdom; empire; realm; dominion, etc. is ruled.
ex: And the Fox guileful, and most covetous; / That neither pleased was, to have the reign / Twixt them divided into even twain

ex: He reigned in an autocratic manner.

ex: The House of Piast reigned Poland from its foundation to 1385.

ex: Silence reigned.
Silence reigned, broken only by the hideous screeching of vultures and the sound of a lawn-mower being used in the hospital grounds.

ety: 1591, re- (“back”) + imburse (“pay”, literally “put in a purse”) (perhaps after Middle French rembourser or Italian rimborsàre), from Middle French embourser, from Old French en- (“in”) + borser (“to get money”), from borse (“purse”), from Medieval Latin bursa (English purse).

s.def: To compensate (someone) with payment; especially, to repay money spent on someone's behalf.
ex: The company will reimburse you for your expenses for the business trip.

s.def: To recoup (funds spent).

ex: expense reimbursement
medical reimbursement

ety: From Middle English rein, reyne, from Anglo-Norman reyne, resne, from Early Medieval Latin retina, ultimately from Classical Latin retineō (“hold back”), from re- + teneō (“keep, hold”). Compare modern French rêne. Displaced native Old English brīdel (“bridle, rein”), Old English wealdleþer, ġewealdleþer (“rein, bridle”, literally “control strap”), Old English sāl (“cord, rein”), Old English tiġel (“rein”), and Old English lāttēh, lāttēh (“leash, rein”).

ex: He mounts and reins his horse.

s.def: To obey directions given with the reins.
ex: She worked each horse at a walk, trot, and then a canter. The horses reined well and executed stops quickly.

ex: I am he which searcheth the reins and hearts.

ex: a reincarnation of an old video game

ety: From Middle English reyndere, reynder, rayne-dere, from Old Norse hreindýri (“reindeer”), from hreinn (“reindeer”) + dýr (“animal”). s.def: Any Arctic and subarctic-dwelling deer of the species Rangifer tarandus, with a number of subspecies.
ex: Santa Claus' sleigh is supposedly pulled by nine reindeer
Herds of wandering reindeer are frequently seen, and may even hold up the train while they cross the unfenced line to reach their feeding grounds.

s.def: Any species, subspecies, ecotype, or other scientific grouping of such animals.
To herd or farm reindeer

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- English inforce English reinforce From re- + inforce.

The kidneys.
The lower part of the back.
The loins.
The parts of a vault between the crown and the spring or abutment, including, and having especial reference to, the loading or filling behind the shell of the vault.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- English insurance English reinsurance From re- + insurance.

s.def: Insurance purchased by insurance companies that spreads the risk associated with selling insurance around so the danger of one large monetary loss is minimized. Such insurance and catastrophe bonds are backstops to insurer insolvency from unexpectedly large losses.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- English insure English reinsure From re- + insure.

ex: Re-issue, re-package, re-package / Re-evaluate the songs / Double pack with a photograph / Extra track and a tacky badge

In patent law: to permit a patent with ministerial errors to be corrected and enforced for the remainder of the original term of the patent.
Something that has issued, or been issued again.
ex: Copies of the original comic are valued by collectors, but the reissues are worthless.

ety: From Late Middle English rejecten, from Latin reiectus, past participle of reicere (“to throw back”), from re- (“back”) + iacere (“to throw”). Displaced native Old English āweorpan (literally “to throw out”).

A rejected defective product in a production line.
A rejected takeoff.

ex: They simply cannot deliver what they promised. Nor will an affronted, alienated Brussels help them do so. Rejigged single market access? Forget it.

s.def: To provide (a place, etc.) with new equipment or machinery; to reequip, to refit.
To separate or sort (ore) again in a jigger or sieve.

ety: From Middle English rejoicen, rejoisen, from Old French resjoir. Doublet of rejoy. Compare French réjouir; Spanish regocijar; Portuguese regozijar; Italian gioire

s.def: to be happy
To be very happy, be delighted, exult; to feel joy.
ex: Leicester closed out the win to spark emotional scenes as those inside Wembley rejoiced in a landmark victory.

s.def: To have (someone) as a lover or spouse; to enjoy sexually.
To make happy, exhilarate.
ex: Were he [Cain] alive, it would rejoice his soul to see what mischief it had made.

s.def: To enjoy.
present participle and gerund of rejoice
An act of showing joy.
ex: There was much rejoicing when the good news finally arrived.

ety: From Middle English rejoynen, partly from Middle French rejoin- (stem of rejoindre, from re- (“again”) + joindre (“to join”)) and partly from re- + joynen. By surface analysis, re- + join. Doublet of rejoinder.

To come, or go, again into the presence of; to join the company of again.
ex: Williams had a problem fitting his left rear tyre and that left Alonso only 3.1secs adrift when he rejoined from his final stop three laps later.

ex: "Be careful what you do," rejoined another man's voice that I did not know, "lest someone see you digging, and scent us out."
