To answer, as the defendant to the plaintiff's replication.
To re-insert a patent claim, typically after allowance of a patent application, applied to patent claims that had been withdrawn from examination under a restriction requirement, based on rejoinder.

ety: From Middle English rejoinder, rejonder, rejoynder, from Middle French rejoindre, with infinitive used as noun frequent in Law French. Doublet of rejoin.

s.def: The defendant's answer to the replication.
A response that answers another response.
A quick response that involves disagreement or is witty, especially an answer to a question.
ex: "I'm starting to-morrow. This is perhaps the last time we shall ever meet." I made an appropriate rejoinder, and he smiled wanly.

s.def: Re-insertion, typically after allowance of a patent application, of patent claims that had been withdrawn from examination under a restriction requirement.
To issue a rejoinder.
To say as a rejoinder.

ety: From re- (“again”) + Latin iuvenis (“young”) + -ate (verb-forming suffix). Compare Old French rejuvener. Displaced native Middle English gingen, from Old English *ġinġan (literally “to make young”), equivalent to Old English ġeong + Old English -an.

s.def: To render young again.
To give new energy or vigour to; to revitalise.
ex: The exercise involved in recrafting the past, past encounters and memories actually rejuvenates short-term and present memory — remarkably!
"We have completely rejuvenated the project. Everyone is galvanised. We will get it open - and open means open. [...]."

ety: From Latin relapsus, past participle of relabi (“to slide back, fall back”), from re- (“back”) + labi (“to slip, slide, fall”).

ex: He has improved recently but keeps relapsing into states of utter confusion.
to relapse into a stupor, into vice, or into barbarism
to relapse into slumber after being disturbed

ex: relapsed after 5 months of being clean

ex: You slip your hold and change your side, Relapsing from a necessary guide.

One who has relapsed, or fallen back into error; a backslider.

ety: From Latin relātus, perfect passive participle of referō (“carry back; report”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Doublet of refer. See also infer, collate and confer, delate and defer, as well as prefer and prelate among others.

To have a connection.

To identify with; to understand.
ex: I find it difficult to relate to others because I'm extremely introverted.

s.def: To bring back; to restore.

s.def: Standing in relation or connection.

on a related note

s.def: Being a relative of.

s.def: Narrated; told.
Synonym of relative.
Fulfilling a relation.

s.def: simple past and past participle of relate

ety: From Middle English relacion, relacioun, from Anglo-Norman relacioun and Old French relacion (whence French relation), from Latin relātiō, noun of process form from perfect passive participle relātus (“related”), from verb referō (“to refer, to relate”), from prefix re- (“again”) + ferō (“to bear, to carry”). By surface analysis, relate + -ion. Doublet of relazione.

s.def: A member of one's extended family; a relative.
ex: Yes, he's a relation of mine, but only a distant one.

s.def: The act of relating a story.
ex: Your relation of the events is different from mine.
I shall you make relacyon By way of apostrofacyon […] How I, Skelton laureat, Devysed and also wrate Uppon a lewde curate, […]

s.def: The manner in which two things may be associated.
ex: The relation between diet and health is complex.
There's no linear relation between mortality and size.

s.def: A relationship; the manner in which and tone with which people or states, etc. interact.
ex: the foreign relations of the United States

s.def: A set of ordered tuples.
ex: Equality is a symmetric relation, while divisibility is not.

s.def: A set of tuples, implemented as a table in a relational database.
ex: This relation uses the customer's social security number as a key.

s.def: A statement of equality of two products of generators, used in the presentation of a group.
A subobject of a product of objects.
The act of intercourse.

have sexual relations with

Relating to relations.

s.def: Friendly and peaceful.
Dealing with the whole of human relations and their social context, rather than an independent and private space.
ex: relational art

s.def: Pertaining to a relational adjective, i.e. an adjective that relates what it modifies to a noun rather than qualifying it.
A database model that is based on first-order predicate logic.

s.def: A connection or association; the condition of being related.

s.def: Kinship; being related by blood or marriage.
A romantic or sexual involvement.
ex: They have been in a relationship for ten years, but have never married.

s.def: The links between the x-values and y-values of ordered pairs of numbers especially coordinates.
A way in which two or more people behave and are involved with each other.
ex: Near-synonym: footing
I have a good working relationship with my boss.

s.def: The level or degree of affinity between keys, chords and tones.

ety: From Middle French relatif, from Late Latin relātīvus, from Latin relātus, perfect passive participle of referō (“to carry back, to ascribe”), from re- (“again”) + ferō (“to bear or carry”). By surface analysis, relate + -ive.

Relevant; pertinent; related.

Food or drink that may be consumed as a meal.

The consumption of food; also, refreshment obtained from eating; (generally) refreshment; rest.
ex: The silk pavilions of King Arthur raised / For brief repast or afternoon repose / By couriers gone before; […]

s.def: To supply (an animal or person) with food; to feed.
To provide (a person) with intellectual or spiritual nourishment; to enlighten, to feed.
To refresh (oneself or someone) through eating and drinking.
Usually followed by on or upon: to take food and drink; to feast, to feed.
ex: [O]n arrival of the dinner-hour, repasteth on domestic fare, (making especial mention of certain fishes, and concluding with cheese,) […]

ety: Borrowed from Latin repatriare, from re- + patria (“homeland”). Cognate to repair (“to return”).

s.def: A person who has returned to their country of origin or whose original citizenship has been restored.
To restore (a person) to their own country.
To return or restore (artworks, museum exhibits, etc.) to their country of origin.
ex: Greece repatriated an Athenian frieze from France, arranging for it to be sent back to Athens.
France repatriated an Athenian frieze back to Greece.

s.def: To convert a foreign currency into the currency of one's own country.

ety: From Old French repaier (“to pay back”), from re- + paiier (“to pay”), from Latin pācāre (“to settle, to make peaceful”), from pāx (“peace”) + -ō (forming verbs). Equivalent to re- + pay. Cognate with repacify and French repayer (“to pay again”).

s.def: Synonym of pay back in all senses.
ex: I finally repaid my student loans, just before sending my kids to college.
I'll repay this wrong asap.
But drops of Grief can ne’re repay / The debt of Love I owe, […]

s.def: To make worthwhile; to yield a result worth the effort; to pay off.
ex: The possible importance of excessive androgen secretion and the ingestion of agents such as the fluorenamines may repay further investigation.

s.def: To give in return; requite.
To pay (cover with tar, pitch, etc.) again.

ety: From Anglo-Norman repeler, from Old French rapeler (“to call back, call in, call after, revoke”), from Latin repellō (“drive or thrust back”), from re- and pellō (“push or strike”). Doublet of repel.

s.def: To cancel, invalidate, annul.
ex: to repeal a law
Labour says it will repeal the legislation if it wins the next General Election.

s.def: To recall; to summon (a person) again; to bring (a person) back from exile or banishment.
ex: The banish’d Bolingbroke repeals himself, And with uplifted arms is safe arrived […]

s.def: To suppress; to repel.
An act or instance of repealing.

ety: From Middle English repeten, from Old French repeter, from Latin repetō, from the prefix re- (“again”) + petō (“to attack, beseech”).

s.def: To do or say again (and again).
ex: The scientists repeated the experiment in order to confirm the result.
I'll tell you my secret, but first promise me you won't repeat it to anyone else!
I don't mind talking about the incident, but one gets tired of repeating themself after the hundredth time.

s.def: To refill (a prescription).
To happen again; recur.
ex: A day like that has not yet repeated itself.

s.def: To echo the words of (a person).
ex: Their rationale with repeating me was that the prior program had not been of sufficient quality to teach me the error of my ways.

s.def: To strike the hours, as a watch does.
To make trial of again; to undergo or encounter again.
ex: He[…] repeats the danger of the burning town.

s.def: To repay or refund (an excess received).
To call in a previous artillery fire mission with the same ammunition and method either on the coordinates or adjusted either because destruction of the target was insufficient or missed.
ex: Add 100, left 50. Repeat, over.
Use "say again" instead of repeat on the radio. Repeat will bring in artillery fire.

s.def: To commit fraud in an election by voting more than once for the same candidate.
An iteration; a repetition.
ex: We gave up after the third repeat because it got boring.

ety: Etymology tree English repeat Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzios Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor. Proto-Germanic *-ārijaz Proto-West Germanic *-ārī Old English -ere Middle English -ere English -er English repeater From repeat + -er.

s.def: One who or that which repeats.
A student repeating a course, class, or grade.
A patient who repeatedly presents with the same symptoms.
A consumer who repeatedly purchases the same goods or services.
One who votes more than once at an election.
A person who regularly sees unexplained sightings of paranormal phenomena.
A gun that has a store of cartridges and does not need reloading after each shot.
A telegraphic instrument for automatically retransmitting a message.
An electronic device that receives a weak or low-level signal and retransmits it at a higher level or higher power.
A watch with a striking apparatus which, upon pressure of a spring, will indicate the time, usually in hours and quarters.

ety: From Middle English repellen, a borrowing from Old French *repeller, from Latin repellere (“to drive back”), from re- (“back”) + pellere (“to drive”). Doublet of repeal.

s.def: To turn (someone) away from a privilege, right, job, etc.
To reject, put off (a request, demand etc.).
To ward off (a malignant influence, attack etc.).
To drive back (an assailant, advancing force etc.).
ex: In nearby Zintan, rebels repelled an advance by Gaddafi's forces, killing eight and taking one prisoner, a local activist said.

s.def: To force away by means of a repulsive force.
To cause repulsion or dislike in; to disgust.
ex: However, while the idea of a free holiday appeals enormously, I am frankly repelled by the idea of spending a couple of weeks in your company.

s.def: To save (a shot).

ety: From Middle English repenten, from Old French repentir, from Vulgar Latin *repaenitīre, from Late Latin paenitīre, from Classical Latin paenitēre. Compare Modern French repentir.

s.def: To feel pain, sorrow, or regret for what one has done or omitted to do; the cause for repenting may be indicated with "of".
ex: Marry in haste, repent at leisure.
If Aljunied decides to go that way (to vote for Workers' Party), well Aljunied has five years to live and repent.

s.def: To be sorry for sin as morally evil, and to seek forgiveness; to cease to practice sin and to love.
ex: I tell you, Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish.
Mad Prophet: Repent! Repent and restore your souls to glory before it is too late! This great station has fallen, and all within shall fall with it!

s.def: To feel pain on account of; to remember with sorrow.
ex: If Aljunied decides to go that way (to vote for the Workers' Party), well Aljunied has five years to live and repent.

s.def: To cause to have sorrow or regret.
ex: at that time she wolde nat, she seyde, for she was syke and myght nat ryde. "That me repentith," seyde the kynge[…].
And it repented the Lord that he had made man on the earth, and it grieved him at his heart.

s.def: to feel sorry for, to regret
To be sorry for, to regret.
ex: I repent my sins.

s.def: To cause (oneself) to feel pain or regret.
To change one's mind.
Creeping along the ground.
ex: The pennated, repent and ferine entities of the boscage, are ousels, shellducks, […] and ursine quadrupeds.

der: marry in haste, repent at leisure

ety: First attested circa 14th century, from Middle English repentance, repentaunce, from Old French repentance. More at repent. By surface analysis, repent + -ance.

s.def: The condition of being repentant, penitent, a state of feeling regret or remorse for having done wrong.
ex: And here, shipmates, is true and faithful repentance; not clamorous for pardon, but grateful for punishment.

s.def: The action of repenting, an instance of it, atonement.
ex: Christine Cooper: It's not wrong to sin. Christ came into this world for the sinners. DCI Tom Barnaby: To call people to repentance, Mrs Cooper.

ety: From re- + people.

s.def: To repopulate.
ex: they issued forth of the mountaines, to repeople the world againe, which they found replenished onely with Serpents.

ety: From Middle French répercussion, from Latin repercussio (“rebounding; repercussion”), from repercutio (“cause to rebound, reflect, strike against”), from re- + percutio (“beat, strike”), from per- (“thoroughly”) + quatio (“shake”).

s.def: A consequence or ensuing result of some action.
ex: You realize this little stunt of yours is going to have some pretty serious repercussions.

s.def: Rapid reiteration of the same sound.
The subsidence of a tumour or eruption by the action of a repellent.
The act of driving back, or the state of being driven back; reflection; reverberation.
ex: the repercussion of sound
Ever echoing back in endless repercussion.

s.def: In a vaginal examination, the act of imparting through the uterine wall with the finger a shock to the foetus, so that it bounds upward, and falls back again against the examining finger.

ety: Borrowed from French répertoire, from Middle French repertoire, from Late Latin repertōrium (“an inventory, list, repertory”). Doublet of repertory.

s.def: A list of dramas, operas, pieces, parts, etc., which a company or a person has rehearsed and is prepared to perform or display.
ex: The conjurer expanded his repertoire with some new tricks.

s.def: The set of skills, abilities, experiences, etc., possessed by a person.
The set of vocalisations used by a bird.
An amount, body, or collection of something.
A processor's instruction set.
An abstract set of characters, independent of their encoding.
ex: ISO Latin 1 repertoire
There is quite a jump from the WGL4 repertoire to the Unicode 2.0 repertoire, but there are few intermediate general purpose repertoires.

ety: Learned borrowing from Late Latin repertōrium. Doublet of repertoire.

s.def: A repertoire.
A collection of things, or a place where such a collection is kept.
A specific set of works that a company performs.
A theater in which a resident company presents works from a specified repertoire, usually in alternation.
A cinema specializing in classic or older films.

ety: Borrowed from Latin repetitionem (accusative singular of repetitio; cf. French répétition). Doublet of repetitio. By surface analysis, repeat + -ition.

s.def: The act or an instance of repeating or being repeated.
The act of performing a single, controlled exercise motion. A group of repetitions is a set.
To petition again.
ex: The group went through several rounds at different courts, petitioning and repetitioning, losing again and again.

s.def: Characterized by repetition, especially excessive repetition.
ex: Near-synonyms: tedious; see also Thesaurus:wearisome

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- English phrase English rephrase From re- + phrase.

s.def: To say or write something with different wording.
ex: Make sure to rephrase your thesis in your conclusion.

ety: Believed to have been formed (with uncertainty, due to the unusual formation) as re- + pine, with the verb giving rise to the noun (first attested in 1529 and 1593 respectively); compare the Middle English verb repinen (“(uncertain) to cause trouble to someone, grieve”) (from pīnen (“to cause pain, grieve, hurt, trouble; to starve, pine; to torment, torture”), from Old English pīnian), which may be related.

s.def: To long for (something) discontentedly; to pine.
ex: But the oath supremacy was not refused, the worship of the church was frequented by multitudes who secretly repined for a change; […]
Yet oft do we repine / For the days of old, / For the days of gold— / For the days of Forty-Nine
Each normal life repines for better life; […]

s.def: To complain; to regret; to fret.
ex: [N]o more need men on earth repine
Beatrix invited me no more to tea but I did not greatly repine.

s.def: A repining.

ety: From Middle English replenisshen, borrowed from Old French repleniss-, stem of some of the conjugated forms of replenir, from re- + plenir, from plein, from Latin plenus.

s.def: To refill; to renew; to supply again or to add a fresh quantity to.
ex: It's a popular product, and they have to replenish their stock of it frequently.

s.def: To fill up; to complete; to supply fully.
To finish; to complete; to perfect.
ex: We smothered the most replenished sweet work of nature.

ety: From Middle English replete (adjective) and repleten (verb), from Old French replet, from Latin repletus.

s.def: Abounding, amply provided.
ex: A kitchen replete with all the ultimate appliances.
A peacock reign'd, whose glorious sway His subjects with delight obey: His tail was beauteous to behold, Replete with goodly eyes and gold.
I am less unhappy than the rest, because I have a mind replete with images.

s.def: Gorged, filled to near the point of bursting, especially with food or drink.
ex: And what an afternoon! To lie, after this feast, on their bellies in the grass, replete like animals […]
In the evening, replete with deer meat, resting on his elbow and smoking his after-supper cigarette, he said[…]

s.def: Isomorphism-closed: Inheriting all the isomorphisms of C. Formally: such that for any isomorphism f in C, if f 's source is in S, then f and f 's target is also in S.
A honeypot ant.
To fill to repletion, or restore something that has been depleted.

ety: Anglo-Norman, from Old French replevir (“recover”), from re- + plevir (apparently from a Germanic word which was also the source of English pledge).

s.def: An action to recover personal property unlawfully taken, especially that seized by way of distraint; the writ or procedure of such action.
To replevy.

ety: Old French replevir (“recover”), from re- + plevir (probably from a Germanic source which also gave pledge).

s.def: To return goods to their rightful owner by replevin; to recover goods.
To bail.
ex: I humbly crave your Majestie / It to replevie , and my Sonne reprive

s.def: replevin

ety: Borrowed from Italian replica, derived from Latin replicare (“to fold or bend back; to reply”). Doublet of reply and replicate.

s.def: An exact copy.
ex: The statue on the museum floor is an authentic replica.

s.def: A copy made at a smaller scale than the original.
ex: He collected replicas of old cars.

ety: From Latin replicātus, past participle of replicāre (“to fold or bend back; reply”), from re (“back”) + plicāre (“to fold”); see ply. Doublet of reply and replica.

s.def: To make a copy (replica) of.
ex: On entering a host cell, a virus will start to replicate.

s.def: To repeat (an experiment or trial) with a consistent result.
To reply.
The outcome of a replication procedure; an exact copy or replica.
A tone that is one or more octaves away from a given tone.
Folded over or backward; folded back upon itself.
ex: a replicate leaf or petal
the replicate margin of a shell

ety: Inherited from Middle English replicacioun, replicacion, from Anglo-Norman replicacioun and Old French replicacion (“reply, answer”), from Latin replicātiō, replicātiōnem. By surface analysis, replicate + -(at)ion.

s.def: The process of producing replicas of DNA or RNA molecules.
The process by which an object, person, place or idea may be copied mimicked or reproduced.
ex: DNA replication is the process of producing two identical replicas from one original DNA molecule.

s.def: Copy; reproduction.
ex: That painting is an almost exact replication of a famous Rembrandt painting.

s.def: A response from the plaintiff to the defendant's plea.

The process of frequent electronic data copying a one database in one computer or server to a database in another so that all users share the same level of information. Used to improve fault tolerance of the system.

ety: From replicate + -or.

s.def: A technological device that replicates physical objects.
ex: Why, this planet was still centuries away from developing such necessities as personal replicators or portable nano-intelligences...

s.def: Something capable of self-replication, like a gene or meme.
ex: We, alone on earth, can rebel against the tyranny of the selfish replicators.

ety: From Middle English replyen, replien, borrowed from Old French replier (“to reply”), from the Latin replicō, replicāre (“to fold back”) (in Late or Medieval Latin "to reply, repeat"), from re + plicō (“to fold”); the noun derives from the verb by nominalisation. Doublet of replicate and replica.

s.def: To give a written or spoken response, especially to a question, request, accusation or criticism; to answer.
ex: (intransitive) Please reply to my letter.
(transitive) "Sorry I'm late," replied the student.
(transitive) He replied that he was not sure.

s.def: To act or gesture in response.
ex: Joanne replied to Pete's insult with a slap to his face.
[…] bulged the onion bag for the Blades, and Downes and Prendergast replied for the Owls.

s.def: To repeat something back; to echo.
A written or spoken response; part of a conversation.
ex: For example, it is said that someone at a party once asked the famous philosopher Ly Tin Weedle ‘Why are you here?’ And the reply took three years.

s.def: Something given in reply.
A counterattack.
The answer of a figure.
A document written by a party specifically replying to a responsive declaration and in some cases an answer.

ety: From Middle English reporten, from Anglo-Norman reporter, from Latin reportāre (“to carry back, return, remit, refer”), from re- + portāre.

s.def: To relate details of (an event or incident); to recount, describe (something).
To notify someone of (particular intelligence, suspicions, illegality, misconduct etc.); to make notification to relevant authorities; to submit a formal report of.
ex: For insurance reasons, I had to report the theft to the local police station.

s.def: A piece of information describing, or an account of certain events given or presented to someone, with the most common adpositions being by (referring to creator of the report) and on (referring to the subject).
ex: A report by the telecommunications ministry on the phone network revealed a severe capacity problem.

s.def: To repeat (something one has heard), to retell; to pass on, convey (a message, information etc.).
To take oneself (to someone or something) for guidance or support; to appeal.
To make a formal statement, especially of complaint, about (someone).
ex: If you do that again I'll report you to the boss.

s.def: To show up or appear at an appointed time; to present oneself.
To write news reports (for); to cover as a journalist or reporter.
ex: Andrew Marr reports now on more in-fighting at Westminster.
Every newspaper reported the war.

s.def: To be accountable to or subordinate to (someone) in a hierarchy; to receive orders from (someone); to give official updates to (someone who is above oneself in a hierarchy).
ex: The financial director reports to the CEO.
Now that I've been promoted, I report to Benjamin, whom I loathe.
Although she was junior to [Barret] Zoph, the report said that she did not report directly to him.

s.def: To return or present as the result of an examination or consideration of any matter officially referred.
ex: The committee reported the bill with amendments, or reported a new bill, or reported the results of an inquiry.

s.def: A document, on cardboard or plain paper, indicating the grades that a student has earned, issued at the end of a term of a regular period.
ex: And with that in mind, I'm going to distribute your report cards. Now, is there a Christian Stobich in this class?

s.def: An update on progress with regard to a policy or system.
A grammatical construction used to represent another person's words, thoughts, or statements indirectly rather than by quoting them verbatim, often involving a change in tense.

ety: From Middle English reportour, from Old French reporteur; equivalent to report + -er.

s.def: A journalist who investigates, edits and reports news stories for newspapers, radio and television.
Someone or something that reports.
ex: The reporters of important security bugs may be paid a bounty by the software developer.

s.def: A person who records and issues official reports of judicial or legislative proceedings.
A case reporter; a bound volume of printed legal opinions from a particular jurisdiction.

A gene attached by a researcher to a regulatory sequence of another gene of interest, typically used as an indication of whether a certain gene has been taken up by or expressed in the cell or organism population.

ety: From report(er) + -orial.

s.def: Of, pertaining to or characteristic of a reporter.
ex: So there I was, in the front row of course (it was my reportorial duty), with a bunch of gay men and straight women.
A master of simple, solid, apoetical, reportorial English.
Among the customers, a columnist for the local newspaper was having lunch and a beer or two, though he could not restrain his reportorial instincts.

ety: The verb is derived from Middle English reposen (“to rest”), from Anglo-Norman reposer, reposir, and Middle French reposer, from Old French reposer, repauser (“to become calm; to be peaceful; to rest; to be immobile; to lie or be placed; to cease, stop; to neglect”) (modern French reposer), from Latin repausāre, the present active infinitive of repausō (“(Late Latin) to be at rest; to lie down, rest; to sleep; to calm, pacify; (Latin) to halt temporarily, pause”), from re- (prefix meaning ‘agai…

s.def: To lay (someone, or part of their body) down to rest.
ex: [T]he eyes clos'd— / The lashes on the cheeks repos'd.
Mrs. Peters reposed her 200 pounds on the safer of the two chairs and gazed stolidly out the one window at the brick wall opposite.

s.def: To rest (oneself), especially by going to sleep.
Followed by from or (obsolete) of: to cause (oneself) to take a rest from some activity; also, to allow (oneself) to recover from some activity.
To give (someone) rest; to refresh (someone) by giving rest.
ex: On the twentieth of June he [Johann de Kalb] entered North Carolina, and halted at Hillsborough to repose his wayworn soldiers.
[D]istant banks of purple mist coloured the liquid plain with a cool green-blue, a celadon tint that reposed the eye and the brain.

s.def: To cause (oneself) to have faith in or rely on someone or something.
To give (someone) accommodation for the night.
To lean or recline, sit down, or lie down to rest; to rest.
ex: Then the divine night came, and treading earth, / Close by the flood that had from Jove her birth, / Within a thicket I repos’d; […]
At night when I reposed, fair dreams did pass / Before my pillow;— […]

s.def: Followed by on or upon: of a thing: to lie or be physically positioned on something, especially horizontally; to rest on or be supported by something.
ex: a trap reposing on sand

s.def: Followed by on or upon: of light, a look, etc.: to fall or rest (and often remain for a while) on something; to alight, to dwell.
ex: [T]he grate did then unclose, / And on that reverend form the moonlight did repose.
For on such things the memory reposes / With tenderness,— […]

s.def: Followed by on or upon: to be based on; to depend or rely on.

ety: Borrowed from Latin repositus, past participle of repōnō (“put back”), from re- + pōnō (“put”). See position.

s.def: To cause to rest or stay in a certain place; to place, put, or deposit.
ex: Others reposit their young in holes.

s.def: To posit again.
ex: Heidegger reposited the question which had earlier been posited by the doctor of monadology, Leibnitz.

s.def: Alternative form of rep.

ety: From Latin reprehendō (“I hold back, check, blame”), from re- (“back”) + prehendō (“I hold, seize”). Compare French reprendre (“to reprove”).

s.def: To criticize, to reprove.
ex: publicly reprehend
severely reprehend
reprehend misconduct

ety: Borrowed from Late Latin reprehensibilis, from Latin reprehendo; equivalent to reprehend + -ible.

s.def: Blameworthy, censurable, guilty.
Deserving of reprehension.
ex: Scarlett O’Hara was the heroine of the novel/movie Gone with the Wind and the reprehensible sequel Scarlett.
At the inquest, the conduct of guard Austin was described as reprehensible.

s.def: A reprehensible person; a villain.

ety: Borrowed from Latin reprehensio, reprehensionis.

s.def: the act, or an expression, of criticism, censure or condemnation; reprimand

ety: Compare French répréhensif.

s.def: Containing reprehension or reproof.
ex: He stops at Winna's reprehensive stare.

s.def: Reprehensible.
ex: Well, there would not be anything particularly reprehensive in a plaintiff wanting to go to a forum where the verdict would be larger.

ety: From Old French représenter, from Latin repraesentō. Displaced native Old English spelian (“to represent”).

s.def: To present again or anew; to present by means of something standing in the place of; to exhibit the counterpart or image of; to typify.
To portray by mimicry or acting; to act the part or character of.
ex: It has always been his dream to represent Hamlet on Broadway.

s.def: To stand or act in the place of; to perform the duties, exercise the rights, or otherwise act on behalf of.
ex: He sent his agent to represent himself at the meeting.
As he was too ill to accept the award, his brother represented him at the ceremony.
An attorney's job is to represent his client in court

s.def: To act as a representative of (a country, state, district etc.).
ex: They chose a member of Congress to represent their district.

s.def: To portray visually; to delineate.
ex: a landscape can be represented in a picture.
The sculptor represented a horse in bronze.

s.def: To portray to another using language; to show; to give one's own impressions and judgement of.
ex: He represented that he was investigating for the police department.

s.def: To give an account of; to describe.
To serve as a sign or symbol of.
ex: The @ symbol represents the online world.
A dove is often used to represent peace.
A person climbs a mountain, not only "because it is there," but also because it represents a fundamental and personal challenge.

s.def: To bring a certain sensation of into the mind; to cause to be known, felt, or apprehended; to present.
To form or image again in consciousness, as an object of cognition or apprehension (something presentative, which was originally apprehended by direct presentation).

ety: From Late Middle English representacioun, from Old French representacion, from Latin repraesentātiō. By surface analysis, represent + -ation.

s.def: That which represents something else.
ex: The Venus of Willendorf was an early representation of the female body.

s.def: The act of representing.
ex: We are no longer happy with your representation of our company at trade events.

s.def: The appearance(s) of a particular demographic group in a piece of media, particularly in regards to how such appearances are treated.
The lawyers and staff who argue on behalf of another in court.
ex: People who cannot afford representation are eligible for government assistance.

s.def: The ability to elect a representative to speak on one's behalf in government; the role of this representative in government.
ex: The lack of representation in the British parliament was one of the main factors behind the American Revolution.

s.def: An action of some algebraic structure (typically a group or algebra, particularly a Lie algebra) on a vector space, such that each element acts by a linear endomorphism.
A figure, image or idea that substitutes reality.
A theatrical performance.
A statement; a presentation of opinion or position, or an utterance made to influence the opinions or actions of others
An act of representing, i.e. presenting again.
ex: rates of representation to the emergency department

ety: From Middle English representative, from Middle French representatif and its etymon Medieval Latin repraesentātīvus. By surface analysis, represent + -ative; See representation. Displaced native Old English spala (“a representative”).

s.def: Typical; having the same properties or interest as a larger group.
ex: If you took all the fools out of the legislature, it wouldn't be a representative body anymore.

s.def: Representing, showing a likeness.
ex: Are you sure this paper is representative of your child's writing?
the representative faculty of the human imagination

s.def: A delegate.
ex: She served four terms as representative of her local at the national union convention.

s.def: Something standing for something else.
A form of government where the people elect representatives who, on their behalf, propose and approve laws and administer the government.

ety: Ultimately from Latin repressus, the perfect passive participle of reprimō (“to repress”).

s.def: To forcefully prevent an upheaval from developing further.
ex: to repress rebellion or sedition
to repress the first risings of discontent

s.def: To check; to keep back.
To press again.
ex: to repress a vinyl record

s.def: A record pressed again; a repressing.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- English press English repress Proto-Indo-European *-tis Proto-Indo-European *-Hō Proto-Indo-European *-tiHō Proto-Italic *-tiō Latin -tiō Latin -ātiōlbor. Old French -ationbor. Middle English -acioun English -ation English -ion English repression From repress + -ion.

s.def: The act of repressing; state of being repressed.
ex: History shows that when governments fear the truth and increase repression, their days are limited.
The most powerful educative force in the new society was, however, the system of police repression.

s.def: The involuntary rejection from consciousness of painful or disagreeable ideas, memories, feelings, or impulses.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- English press English repress Proto-Indo-European *-wós Proto-Indo-European *-iHwósder. Latin -īvus Old French -ifbor. Middle English -yf English -ive English repressive From repress + -ive.

s.def: Serving to repress or suppress; oppressive
ex: First, the classical rule forbids any unilateral right to use force to overthrow a regime on the sole grounds that it is repressive in character.

ety: First use appears c. 1513 in the writings of Robert Fabyan. In the sense of “to take back to prison”, from Middle English repryen (“to remand, detain”) (1494), possibly from Middle French repris, in the form of reprendre (“take back”); a cognate to reprise. The sense has become generalized, but does retain connotations of punishment and execution. The noun's first use appears c. 1592.

s.def: To cancel or postpone the punishment of someone, especially an execution.
To bring relief to someone.
ex: Company […] may reprieve a man from his melancholy, yet it cannot secure him from his conscience.

s.def: To take back to prison (in lieu of execution).
To abandon or postpone plans to close, withdraw or abolish (something).
The cancellation or postponement of a punishment.
ex: The prisoner was saved from execution; the governor had requested a reprieve.

s.def: A document authorizing such an action.
Relief from pain etc., especially temporary.
A cancellation or postponement of a proposed event undesired by many.
ex: And it said there was no reprieve for 435 stations already approved for closure before the report appeared.

ety: From French réprimande, from réprimer (“to repress”).

s.def: A severe, formal or official reproof; reprehension, rebuke, private or public.
ex: Goldsmith gave his landlady a sharp reprimand for her treatment of him.

s.def: To reprove in a formal or official way.

ety: From re- + print (verb).

s.def: A book, pamphlet or other printed matter that has been published once before but is now being released again.
ex: The reprint is much less expensive than a first edition.

s.def: To print (something) that has been published in print before.
ex: The novel was printed with an appendix.

s.def: To renew the impression of.
ex: The whole business of our redemption is […] to reprint God's image upon the soul.

ety: From Anglo-Norman reprisaille (French représaille), from Old Italian ripresaglia (Italian rappresaglia), from ripreso, past participle of riprendere (“to take back”), from Latin reprendere, earlier reprehendere (see reprehend).

s.def: An act of retaliation.
Something taken from an enemy in retaliation.
The act of taking something from an enemy by way of retaliation or indemnity.
ex: debatable ground, on which incursions and reprisals continued to take place

ety: From Middle English reprise (noun) and reprisen (verb), from Old French reprise, from reprendre. In some senses borrowed anew from Modern French reprise.

s.def: A recurrence or resumption of an action.
A repetition of a phrase, a return to an earlier theme, or a second rendition or version of a song in a programme or musical.
A renewal of a failed attack, after going back into the en garde position.
Deductions and duties paid yearly out of a manor and lands, as rent charge, pensions, annuities, etc.; also spelled reprizes.
A ship recaptured from an enemy or from a pirate.
In masonry, the return of a moulding in an internal angle.
A taking by way of retaliation.
To take (something) up or on again.
ex: How to take life from that dead-liuing swaine, / Whom still he marked freshly to arize / From th'earth, & from her wombe new spirits to reprize.

s.def: To repeat or resume an action or a role.
ex: The aging actress played the role she played in her youth, as if to reprise it.

s.def: To recompense; to pay.

s.def: A mild rebuke, or an implied criticism.
ex: My father made no reproach in his letters and only took notice of my science by inquiring into my occupations more particularly than before.

s.def: To criticize or rebuke (someone).

this new commer, Shame, There sit not, and reproach us as unclean.

ety: From reproach + -ful.

s.def: Expressing or containing reproach

ex: He lived a reproachful life.

ety: First attested in c. 1425, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English reprobat(e) (“condemned, damned”, also used as the past participle of reprobaten), borrowed from Latin reprobātus (“disapproved, rejected, condemned”), perfect passive participle of reprobō, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix). Rejected by God; damned, sinful.
Immoral, having no religious or principled character.

s.def: One rejected by God; a sinful person.

s.def: To have strong disapproval of something; to reprove; to condemn.

To refuse, set aside.

s.def: A method for reproducing a bug or problem.

ety: From Old French reprove, from reprover. See reprove.

s.def: An act or instance of reproving or of reprobating; a rebuke, a reproach, an admonition.
ex: You could not give me a greater reproof for the mistake I fell into. It was all my doing, I know. I have not forgotten it, I assure you.

s.def: To proof again.

ety: From Middle English repreven, reproven, from Anglo-Norman reprover, Middle French reprouver, from Latin reprobāre. Doublet of reprobate.

s.def: To express disapproval.
To criticise, rebuke, or reprimand (someone), usually in a gentle and kind tone.
To deny or reject (as a feeling, behaviour, action, etc.).
ex: She ached to be with Affad again – and to reprove the feeling she frowned and bit her lip.

s.def: To prove again.
ex: As we've just learned, as long as we live in the manifest realm, a hero's journey is never over. We are constantly having to reprove ourselves.

ety: From Middle English reptil, from Old French reptile, from Late Latin rēptile, neuter of reptilis (“creeping”), from Latin rēpō (“to creep”), from Proto-Indo-European *rep- (“to creep, slink”) (Pokorny; Watkins, 1969).

Any member of the class Reptilia, including birds.
Any creeping or crawling animal, one that moves along close to the ground on its belly or on short legs, such as a lizard, snake, salamander, frog, toad, or scorpion.

ex: Prior to the 1990s, the non-mammalian synapsids were considered true reptiles.
mammal-like reptile

s.def: An abject, grovelling, loathsome or repulsive person.

s.def: Creeping; moving on the belly, or by means of small and short legs.

ex: a reptile race or crew reptile vices

ety: First attested in 1543; from Latin repudiātus, the perfect passive participle of repudiō (“to cast off, reject”) (see -ate (etymology 1, 2 and 3)), from repudium (“rejection, repudiation, divorce”).

s.def: To cause revulsion in; to repel.
ex: The smell of rotting food repulsed me.

s.def: The act of repulsing or the state of being repulsed.
Refusal, rejection or repulsion.

ety: From Old French reputer, from Latin reputō (“to count over, reckon, calculate, compute, think over, consider”), from re- (“again”) + putō (“to think”).

To attribute or credit something to something; to impute.
To consider, think, esteem, reckon (a person or thing) to be, or as being, something
ex: Wherefore are we counted as beasts, and reputed vile in your sight?

ety: From Middle English request, from Old French requeste (French requête), from Vulgar Latin *requaesita, from Latin requīsīta, feminine of requīsītus (“requested, demanded”), past participle of requīrō (“require, ask”), composed of re- + quaerō (“to seek, look for”), of uncertain origin, but possibly from Proto-Italic *kʷaizeō, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷeh₂- (“to acquire”). s.def: To ask for (something).

s.def: That which is asked for or requested.

ety: Etymology tree English requite Proto-Indo-European *h₂el- Proto-Indo-European *-is Proto-Indo-European *h₂élisder.? Proto-Italic *-ālis Latin -ālisbor. Old French -albor. ▲ Latin -ālis Old French -elbor. ▲ Latin -ālisbor. Middle English -al English -al English requital From requite + -al. First attested in 1545.

s.def: Compensation for damage or loss; amends.
Retaliation or reprisal; vengeance.
Return in kind; recompense, repayment, reward.
ex: O, take his mother's thanks, a widow's thanks, / Till your strong hand shall help to give him strength / To make a more requital to your love.
But we are thinking here above all of the happiness that comes with the requital of love, of the case in which my love is returned with an equal love.

ety: The verb is derived from Middle English requiten (“to repay”), and then partly from both of the following: * From re- (prefix meaning ‘again; back, backward’) + quiten (“to pay, pay for; to repay; to acquit (someone of a charge), exonerate; to prove (oneself) innocent; to answer, reply; to atone for (a sin); to compensate, make amends; to depart, leave; to equal, match; to fulfil (an obligation); to give back, return; to give up, relinquish; to release, set free; to render (a service); to rewar…

s.def: To repay (a debt owed); specifically, to recompense or reward someone for (a favour, a service rendered, etc.)
ex: Children are disobedient, and they sting / Their father's hearts to madness and despair / Requiting years of care with contumely.
Good cryptographists are rare indeed; and thus their services, although seldom required, are necessarily well requited.

s.def: To repay (someone) a debt owed; specifically, to recompense or reward (someone) for a favour, a service rendered, etc.
ex: Well, Edie, we have enough to pay our debts, let folks say what they will, and requiting you is one of the foremost—let me press this sum upon you.

s.def: To respond to or reciprocate (feelings, especially affection or love which has been shown).
To do or give a thing in return for (something).
To retaliate or seek revenge for (an insult, a wrong, etc.).; to avenge.
To retaliate or seek revenge against (someone) for an insult, a wrong, etc.; also (reflexive, rare), to seek revenge for (oneself).
ex: And for a world bestowed, or a friend lost, / He can feel hate, fear, shame; not gratitude: / He but requites me for his own misdeed.

s.def: To greet (someone) in return.
To make up for (something); to compensate.
To respond to (a question, a statement, etc.).
To take the place of (someone or something); to replace.

ety: From Middle English reredos, from Anglo-Norman reredos, areredos; equivalent to rere (“rear”) + French dos (“back”).

s.def: A screen or decoration behind the altar in a church, usually depicting religious iconography or images, akin to the iconostasis of the Eastern Churches.
ex: Near-synonym: retable (often synonymous)
There seem to be no remains of wooden reredoses of the fourteenth century, though there are a number of examples in stone.

s.def: The back of an open fire-hearth, in medieval halls and in some later architecture inspired by them.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- English run English rerun From re- + run.

s.def: An act or instance of rerunning; a repetition.
ex: Even some strong supporters of leaving the UK worry that an early re-run would be doomed to failure.

s.def: A television program shown after its initial presentation, particularly many weeks after its initial presentation; a repeat.
ex: I'm not a fan of the new Simpsons episodes, but the old reruns have me in stitches, although I've seen them countless times.

s.def: Another printing run (impression; batch of copies of a given edition) of a book, cartoon, etc.
A political candidate who holds the same political agenda or doctrine as a past or incumbent holder of a given political office.
A second or subsequent run of a computer program.
ex: Each rerun of the algorithm takes several minutes.

s.def: To run again; to repeat.
ex: Ms. Hill has rerun those questions in her mind. “If the girls told me they want to stay where they are, I would have to leave them,” she said.

s.def: To broadcast (a television program etc.) again.
ex: They're still rerunning The Flintstones on this channel.

s.def: To be broadcast again.
To run (a race or other contest) again.
ex: rerun the election

s.def: To run (a computer program) again.
ex: Restart the computer and rerun the installation.

ety: From re + -s.

Clipping of reservation or reserve (semiautonomous Indigenous territory).
Clipping of residence.

Clipping of resurrection.

ex: Your magic res doesn't need to be that high.

ex: You have the skills, right? Res me please.

ety: From the Latin rescindō (“to cut back”), from re- (“back”) + scindō (“to cut”).

s.def: To repeal, annul, or declare void; to take (something such as a rule or contract) out of effect.
ex: The agency will rescind the policy because many people are dissatisfied with it.

s.def: To cut away or off.

ety: 1651, Late Latin rescissio, from Latin rescindō (“to cut back”), from re- (“back”) + scindō (“to cut”).

s.def: An act of rescinding: removing, taking away, or taking back.
The undoing of a contract; repeal.

ety: From Latin rescriptum (“written reply”).

s.def: A copy, or act of rewriting something; a rewrite.
An epistle from the pope responding to some specific question of canon law or morality; a papal decision on a question of doctrine.
A statement issued by an emperor which sets out legal guidance on some matter, especially in response to a formal request from a magistrate or similar.
ex: "'In order that the people may know of my decision, I request you to prepare at once an imperial rescript that I may broadcast to the nation.'"

s.def: Any official edict or announcement.
A duplicate of, or counterpart to, a legal document.
To script again or anew.
ex: We're rescripting some popular British TV shows for an American audience.

ety: From Middle English rescouen, from Old French rescoure, rescurre, rescorre; from Latin prefix re- (“re-”) + excutere (“to shake or drive out”), from ex (“out”) + quatiō (“to shake”). Displaced native Old English nerian.

s.def: To save from any violence, danger or evil.
ex: The well-trained team rescued everyone after the avalanche.
Soon after rescuing some silly children from the local caves, the alien prangs his vessel and dies.

s.def: To free or liberate from confinement or other physical restraint.
ex: to rescue a prisoner from the enemy

s.def: To recover forcibly, especially from a siege.
To remove or withdraw from a state of exposure to evil and sin.
ex: Traditionally missionaries aim to rescue many ignorant heathen souls.

s.def: To achieve something positive under difficult conditions.
ex: Jews rescued some normalcy from increasingly difficult times by assuaging their constant Angst in the family and community and making do with less.

s.def: To restore a particular trait in an organism that was lost or altered, especially where this loss was as the consequence of some experimental manipulation.
To salvage and restore something that has been discarded.
ex: I rescued a set of antique dining chairs.

s.def: To fix a mistake made while preparing something, especially in cooking.
ex: The cook rescued the sauce after it began to curdle.

s.def: To adopt (an animal).
ex: We rescued a dog, Dylan, which would begin my lifelong love of animals, especially dogs.

s.def: An act or episode of rescuing, saving.
ex: Guests marveled that they kept making more rescues.

ety: From rescue + -er.

s.def: A person who rescues someone or something.
ex: As Tarzan’s heavy hand fell upon his shoulder the priest dropped his victim, and turned upon her would-be rescuer.
[…] an opportunistic relative masquerading as his rescuer, […]
By now, a new worry had emerged. With the rescuers working close to so many dead bodies, there was fear of disease taking hold.

ety: Early Modern French rechercher (“to examine closely”), from Old French recerchier (“to seek, to look for”), by surface analysis, re- + search.

s.def: Diligent inquiry or examination to seek or revise facts, principles, theories, applications, etc. (that are currently available, or that are familiar to oneself).
ex: The research station that houses Wang and his team is outside Lijiang, a city of about 1.2 million people.

s.def: A particular instance or piece of research.
ex: The dearest interests of parties have frequently been staked on the results of the researches of antiquaries.
The first step I took in this so necessary a research, was to examine the motives, the justice, the necessity and expediency of the revolution[…]

s.def: To search or examine with continued care; to seek diligently.
To make an extensive investigation into.
To search again.
To receive a certain response in market research.
ex: Agency and bank staff told the newspaper the ad researched well.

s.def: One who researches.

ety: Learned borrowing from Latin resectiō.

A method of determining a position by using a map and compass bearings for two additional points.
A section of a tire that has had worn tread replaced.
ex: A bruised carcass can often be saved by investing $11.00 in a resection.

ety: From French réséda, from Latin resēda, said by Pliny the Elder (23–79 C.E.) to be from resēdāre (“to soothe”), from re- (“again”) + sēdāre (“to assuage, calm”)), an allusion to the healing properties of the plant.

s.def: Any of various plants of the genus Reseda having small, pale grayish green flowers, such as dyer's rocket (Reseda luteola) and mignonette (Reseda odorata).
Mignonette (Reseda odorata).
A pale greyish-green colour like the flowers of a reseda plant; mignonette.
Having a pale greyish-green colour like the flowers of a reseda plant; mignonette.
ex: By mixing a weaker bath than the one indicated the cotton dyes up a dark green, and the wool acquires a dull and weak reseda shade.

ety: From Middle English resemblen, from Anglo-Norman resembler, ressembler, from re- + sembler (“to seem”). By surface analysis, re- + semble.

s.def: to be like or similar to something else
To compare; to regard as similar, to liken.
ex: And th'other all yclad in garments light, / Discolour'd like to womanish disguise, / He did resemble to his Ladie bright [...].

s.def: To counterfeit; to imitate.
ex: They can so well resemble mans speech.

s.def: To cause to imitate or be like; to make similar.
ex: they resemble themselves to the swans

s.def: To be like or similar to (something); to represent as similar.
ex: The twins resemble each other.
But what you've just described does resemble a person of that kind.

s.def: A town in southwestern North Macedonia.

ety: From Middle French ressentir, resentir, from Old French resentir (Modern ressentir), from re- + sentir (“to feel”).

ex: The bride greatly resented being left at the church.
so that they resent recent Kartvelian encroachment on their land, which has been accompanied by repeated attempts to Georgianize them.

ex: Do you resent us for offering you that choice?

ex: […] which makes the tragical ends of noble persons more favorably resented by compassionate readers.

To give forth an odor; to smell; to savor.

ex: Is it serving Hashem to be machmir and resentful, rather than adhere to the letter of the law and be relaxed and happy?

ety: From resent + -ment, after Middle French and French ressentiment (in Old French as recentement), from an archaic usage of the verb ressentir via Old French sentir, from Latin sentiō, sentīre (“to feel”). Compare Italian risentimento, Portuguese ressentimento, and Spanish resentimiento. Doublet of resentiment and ressentiment, the former attested slightly earlier.

The area which separates opposing lanes of traffic on a divided motorway or dual carriageway.

the Clergy Reserves in Canada are for the support of the clergy.

ety: From French réservoir (“collection place”) (fig.), réservoir (“storehouse”) (lit.). in turn from French réserver (“to reserve, keep”).

s.def: A place where anything is kept in store.

A supply or source of something.

A "black box" component that receives an input signal to be read out and mapped by another process, as part of reservoir computing.
To store or keep (something) in or as in a reservoir.

The right to legally reside in a country.

ety: From Middle English resident, from Anglo-Norman resident, from Latin residēns, present participle of resideō (“to remain behind, reside, dwell”), equivalent to reside + -ent, from re- (“back”) + sedeō (“to sit”). (physician): So called because in the 19th century they resided in the hospital dormitories.

A bird which does not migrate during the course of the year.
A physician receiving postgraduate medical training in a hospital or clinic.
ex: She's a resident in neurosurgery at Mass General.

A legal permanent resident, someone who maintains residency.

ex: resident in the city or in the country

one there still resident as day and night

Of or pertaining to a place of personal residence or to a location for such places.
ex: They live in a residential neighborhood.

Of or pertaining to residency.
ex: There is a residential requirement for obtaining a marriage license here.

ex: The youth group organises annual residentials.

s.def: Of, pertaining to, or having residence, especially official residence.
A canon who has an official residence.

ety: Recorded since 1570. From residue, itself borrowed during the Middle English period from Old French residu (Modern French résidu), from Latin residuum (“a remainder”), the neuter inflection of residuus (“remaining, left over”), perfect participle of resideō (“to remain behind”), from re- (“back, again”) + sedeō (“to sit, to reside”).

ex: Yet certain films leave a residual memory—such as Psycho: many people still feel uneasy showering in a motel bathroom.

Payments made to performers, writers and directors when a recorded broadcast is repeated.
The difference between the observed value and the estimated value of the quantity of interest.
A spiritual presence left behind in a place as a result of a person's death or some other significant event.
Of or relating to a residue; residual; left over, when the main portion has been removed.
ex: Between residuary sobs she drank it like water, sitting up, Robert Loo on the bed's edge, his finger-tips on the base of the glass.

One who receives the residue of an estate.

ety: From Middle English residue, from Old French residu, from Latin residuum, neuter of residuus (“remaining”), from resideō (“to remain behind”). Doublet of residuum.

The substance that remains after evaporation, distillation, filtration or any similar process.
A molecule that is released from a polymer after bonds between neighbouring monomers are broken, such as an amino acid in a polypeptide chain.
Whatever property or effects are left in an estate after payment of all debts, other charges and deduction of what is specifically bequeathed by the testator.
A representative element of an equivalence class modulo some base, conventionally in the half-open interval from zero to the base; the nonnegative remainder after dividing a number by a base.
A form of complex number, proportional to the contour integral of a meromorphic function along a path enclosing one of its singularities.
ex: By taking residues, we can represent this integral in terms of a Jackson integral.

ety: From Latin residuum. Doublet of residue.

The solid material remaining after the liquid in which it was dissolved has been evaporated; a residue.
A binary function from [0,1] × [0,1] to [0,1] which is defined in terms of the t-norm as follows: x→y= sup z|z*x⩽y, where * denotes the t-norm function and sup denotes the supremum.
The residue of an estate.

ety: From Anglo-Norman resigner, Middle French resigner, and its source, Latin resignāre (“to unseal, annul, assign, resign”), from re- + signāre (“to seal, stamp”). Piecewise doublet of re-sign.

ex: I am resigning in protest of the unfair treatment of our employees.

To hand over (something to someone), place into the care or control of another.
To submit passively; to give up as hopeless or inevitable.
ex: He had no choice but to resign the game and let his opponent become the champion.

ety: From Middle English resignacion, resignacioun, from Old French resignation, from Medieval Latin resignātiōnem, accusative of resignātio. Equivalent to resign + -ation.

s.def: The act of resigning.
ex: Jane tendered her resignation to the board of directors, but they refused.

ex: hand in one's resignation

s.def: An uncomplaining acceptance of something undesirable but unavoidable.
ex: With resignation I acknowledged that after the accident I would not be able to ski again.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re- Latin saliō Latin resiliō English -ence English resilience From Latin resiliō (“to spring back”) + English -ence.

The physical property of material that can resume its shape after being stretched or deformed; elasticity.

The positive capacity of an organizational system or company to adapt and return to equilibrium after a crisis, failure or any kind of disruption, including: an outage, natural disasters, man-made disasters, terrorism, or similar (particularly IT systems, archives).
The capacity to resist destruction or defeat, especially when under extreme pressure.

ety: Etymology tree Latin resiliō Proto-Indo-European *-onts Latin -ns Latin -ēns Latin resiliēnsder. English resilient From Latin resiliēns, resilientem (“rebounding”, present active participle of resiliō) (whence -ent), from saliō (“leap, jump”).

Returning quickly to original shape after force is applied; elastic. (of objects or substances)
Returning quickly to normal after damaging events or conditions. (of systems, organisms or people)
ex: He’s resilient, and strong, but sometimes tonight, here, the weight of what he’s saying makes him stop, pause as if lost.

ety: Etymology tree Ancient Greek ῥητῑ́νη (rhētī́nē)bor. Latin rēsīnader. Old French résinebor. Middle English resyn English resin From Middle English resyn, resyne, from Old French résine, from Latin resīna. Doublet of rosin.

s.def: A viscous water-insoluble hydrocarbon exudate of certain plants, or such a substance as a component of a plant exudate; used in lacquers, varnishes and many other applications.
ex: Pine trees produce a sticky resin.
But those who attack violists shouldn't throw resin. Once the ergonomic viola catches on what instrument will be immune?

s.def: Any synthetic compound of similar properties.
ex: The artist used synthetic resin in her sculptures.

s.def: To apply resin to.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French résineux; cf. Latin resinosus. By surface analysis, resin + -ous.

s.def: Of or relating to resin.
Negative (of electric charge).

ety: From Middle English resisten, from Middle French resister and Old French resistre, and their source, Latin resistere, from re- + sistere (“cause to stand”).

the resistance of bacteria to certain antibiotics

s.def: A force that tends to oppose motion.
Electrical resistance.
A resistor.
An underground organisation engaged in a struggle for liberation from forceful occupation; a resistance movement.

ety: From French résistant; equivalent to resist + -ant.

s.def: A person who resists; especially a member of a resistance movement.
A thing which resists.
Which makes resistance or offers opposition.
Which is not affected or overcome by a disease, drug, chemical or atmospheric agent, extreme of temperature, etc.
ex: The infection is resistant to antibiotics.

s.def: Not greatly influenced by individual members of a sample.

ety: From Romanian Reșița.

ety: From Late Latin resolubilis, from Latin resolvō.

s.def: Synonym of resolvable.

ety: From Latin resolutus (“released”), past participle of resolvō (“to release, to unbind”) (re- + solvō, whence solve). Compare typologically Russian реши́тельный (rešítelʹnyj) (< реши́ть (rešítʹ)).

ety: Recorded since 1412, as Middle English resolucioun (“dissolution”), either from Anglo-Norman resolucion or directly from Latin resolūtiō (“a loosening, solution”), from resolvō (“to loosen”), itself from the intensive prefix re- + solvō (“to loosen”). s.def: The degree of fineness with which an image can be recorded or produced, often expressed as the number of pixels per unit of length (typically an inch).

s.def: The number of pixels in an image being stored or displayed.

s.def: A statement of intent, a vow.

s.def: The act or process of resolving: solving.

s.def: The degree of fineness of such a separation.

A formal statement adopted by an assembly, or during any other formal meeting.
ex: The resolution was passed by a two-thirds majority.

s.def: A firm decision or an official decision.
An exact sequence of modules (or, objects in the same category as M) either terminating in M or such that M is the homology at degree zero. See Resolution (algebra).

ety: From Middle English resolven, from Old French resolver, a learned borrowing of Latin resolvō (“loosen, thaw, melt, resolve”), equivalent to re- + solve. Piecewise doublet of re-solve.

s.def: To reduce to simple or intelligible notions; to make clear or certain; to unravel; to explain.
ex: to resolve a riddle

To melt; to dissolve; to become liquid.

ety: From Old French resonance (French résonance), from Latin resonantia (“echo”), from resonō (“to resound”).

Something that evokes an association, or a strong emotion; something that strikes a chord.
ex: emotional resonance
