s.def: Synonym of aposiopesis (“an abrupt breaking-off in speech”).

ety: Latin reticēns, present participle of reticeō (“to keep silence”).

s.def: Unwilling to communicate; keeping one's thoughts and opinions to oneself; reserved or restrained.
ex: She's rather reticent on the subject of her finances.
But they were not reticent enough to prevent the circulation of certain uneasy rumours and extravagant stories of discreditable adventures.

s.def: Hesitant or not wanting to take some action; reluctant (usually followed by a verb in the infinitive).
ex: He is reticent to travel so much.
The police may be reticent to charge the alleged offender, prosecutors reticent to continue with the prosecution, and juries reticent to convict.

ety: Borrowed from Late Latin rēticulum, diminutive of Latin rēte (“net”). Doublet of reticulum, Reticulum, and reticule.

s.def: A transparent plate marked with a crosshair, grid, or scale which is used in an optical instrument, etc., to aid in alignment, counting, or measurement of objects being observed; also, the crosshair, grid, or scale on such a plate.
A master or template, comprising a pattern of lines and shapes, used in photolithography to create the tiny integrated circuits on a microchip.
ex: Near-synonym: photomask (broadly synonymous in context)

s.def: Alternative form of reticule (“a little bag”).

ety: Borrowed from New Latin rēticulāris, from Latin rēticulum (“little net”).

s.def: Having the structure of a net or a network; netlike.
Of or pertaining to a reticulum.

ety: Learned borrowing from Latin rēticulātus (“reticulated, net-like”).

s.def: Network-like in form or appearance.
To distribute or move via a network.
To divide into or form a network.
To create a network.

ety: From French réticule, from Latin rēticulum, diminutive of rēte (“net”). Doublet of reticle, reticulum, and Reticulum.

s.def: A reticle; a grid in the eyepiece of an instrument.
ex: [H]er hair had been used to create the reticule in the famous Norden bombsight—a top-secret WWII targeting device.

s.def: A small women's bag made of a woven net-like material.
ex: She carries some small litter in a reticule which she calls her documents, principally consisting of paper matches and dry lavender.
Miss Pross, exploring the depths of her reticule through her tears with great difficulty, paid for her wine.
Eleanor wore a green silk dress to bring out here eyes, with an ivory tatted collar and reticule to match.

ety: Borrowed from Latin rēticulum (“net”). Doublet of reticle, reticule, and Reticulum.

s.def: The second compartment of the stomach of a cow or other ruminant.
ex: As the young ruminant consumes forages, the reticulum, and particularly the rumen, develop rapidly.

s.def: A network. For example, the endoplasmic reticulum forms a network of cellular components that functions as a transportation system within the cell.
A pattern of interconnected objects.
The tripe made from the second compartment of the stomach of a cow (or other ruminant).

ety: From Latin rēticulum (“net”) + -form.

s.def: Having the form of a net; reticulate

ety: From Middle English rethina, borrowing from Medieval Latin rētīna (“retina”, feminine noun), ellipsis of tunica rētīna (“net-like tunic”), used to describe the blood vessel system at the back of the eye. The phrase is attested in the 12th century in Guillelmus the abbot and Gerard of Cremona—the latter may have created this phrase as a translation for Arabic طَبَقَة شَبَكِيَّة (ṭabaqa šabakiyya) "net-like layer", which translates Ancient Greek ἀμφιβληστροειδής χῐτών (amphiblēstroeidḗs khĭtṓn, “…

s.def: The thin layer of cells at the back of the eyeball that contains rods and cones sensitive to light, which trigger nerve impulses that pass via the optic nerve to the brain, where a visual image is formed.

ety: Etymology tree English retina Proto-Indo-European *-tósder. Ancient Greek -της (-tēs)der. Ancient Greek -ῖτις (-îtis)lbor. New Latin -itisder. English -itis English retinitis From retina + -itis.

s.def: Inflammation of the retina.

ety: From retino- + blastoma.

s.def: A malignant tumour of the retina; a hereditary condition found mostly in children.
ex: Retinoblastoma has two distinct variants, an inherited “familial” form and a sporadic form.

ety: From retina + -ol.

s.def: A fat-soluble carotenoid vitamin (vitamin A), present in fish oils and green vegetables, essential to normal vision and to bone development.

ety: From retino- + -pathy.

s.def: Non-inflammatory disease of the retina.
ex: ‘I have diabetic retinopathy, monsieur.’

ety: From Middle English retenue, from Old French retenue, past participle of retenir (“retain”). Doublet of ritenuto.

s.def: A group of attendants or servants, especially of someone considered important.
ex: the queen’s retinues

s.def: A group of warriors or nobles accompanying a king or other leader; comitatus.
A service relationship.

ety: From Middle French retirer (“draw back”), from Old French retirer, built from re- (“back”) + tirer (“draw, pull”), the latter from Vulgar Latin *tīrāre, of highly uncertain origin.

s.def: To stop working on a permanent basis, usually because of old age or illness.
ex: Having made a large fortune, he retired.
He wants to retire at 55.
She decided to retire from her banking job due to stress.

s.def: To stop playing their sport and in competitions a sports player.
ex: I have decided to retire from football at the end of the season after the World Cup.
I have decided to retire from test cricket at 45.

s.def: To withdraw; to take away.
ex: He […] retired himself, his wife, and children into a forest.

s.def: To go back or return; to withdraw or retreat, especially from public view; to go into privacy.
ex: I will retire to the study.
to retire from the world
to retire from the public eye

s.def: To retreat from action or danger; to withdraw for safety or pleasure.
ex: to retire from battle
The regiment retired from the fray after the Major was killed.

s.def: To go to bed.
ex: I will retire for the night.

s.def: To cease use or production of something.
ex: The steamship made thousands of trips over several decades before it was retired by the shipping company.
When a hurricane becomes so deadly or destructive that future use would be insensitive, officials may retire the name of the hurricane.
Only now, due to the COVID-19-associated drop in traffic, are they being retired with 12 of the 30 trains moved to Landore (Swansea) for warm storage.

s.def: To withdraw from circulation, or from the market; to take up and pay.
ex: The central bank retired those notes five years ago.

s.def: To cause to retire; specifically, to designate as no longer qualified for active service; to place on the retired list.
ex: The board retired the old major.

s.def: To voluntarily stop batting before being dismissed so that the next batsman can bat.
ex: Jones retired in favour of Smith.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- Proto-West Germanic *teuʀōn Old English tēorian Middle English tiren English tire English retire English -ed English retired From retire + -ed.

s.def: Of a place, far from civilization, not able to be easily seen or accessed; secluded.
ex: The little stone Saint occupied a retired niche in a side aisle of the old cathedral.

s.def: No longer in use or production.
ex: Following Jackie Robinson's success, his uniform number, 42, became a retired number across all major league teams.

s.def: Secluded from society (of a lifestyle, activity etc.); private, quiet.
ex: I lead a retired lifestyle.

s.def: Having left employment, especially on reaching pensionable age. (of people)
ex: The retired workers are a major expense due to their pensions.

s.def: simple past and past participle of retire

ety: From French retirement, from retirer (“withdraw, retire”); corresponding to retire + -ment.

s.def: The state of being retired; seclusion.
An act of retiring; withdrawal.
A place of seclusion or privacy; a retreat.
ex: When her mother frowned, and her friend looked cool, she would steal to this retirement, where human foot seldom trod […].
[…] and chance had less in its favour in the crowd of London than even in the retirement of Barton […]

s.def: The state of having permanently left one's employment, now especially at reaching pensionable age; the portion of one's life after retiring from one's career.
ex: "I tried retirement ten years ago. Didn't think much of it. Complete waste of time. So I gave it up after two weeks."

s.def: The act of leaving one's career or employment permanently.
introverted, liking privacy and seclusion.
ex: I don't really know him well, since he's so shy and retiring.
My uncle, as I can remember, was retiring in his disposition, scarcely ever visiting any one and not more frequently receiving any visitors.
Lester was in the thick of social and commercial affairs; he walked in paths to which Jennie's retiring soul had never aspired.

s.def: present participle and gerund of retire
ex: Today is the party for our retiring co-workers.

s.def: retirement

ety: From Middle English retorte, from Latin retortus, from retorquēre (“to be forced to twist back”).

s.def: A sharp or witty reply, or one which turns an argument against its originator; a comeback.
ex: He countered her insult with a clever retort.

s.def: To say something sharp or witty in answer to a remark or accusation.
To make a remark which reverses an argument upon its originator; to return, as an argument, accusation, censure, or incivility.
ex: to retort the charge of vanity
And with retorted scorn his back he turned.

s.def: To bend or curve back.
ex: a retorted line
With retorted head, pruned themselves as they floated.

s.def: To throw back; to reverberate; to reflect.
ex: As when his virtues, shining upon others, / Heat them and they retort that heat again / To the first giver.

s.def: A flask with a rounded base and a long neck that is bent down and tapered, used to heat a liquid for distillation.
ex: A large curved retort was boiling furiously in the bluish flame of a Bunsen burner, and the distilled drops were condensing into a two-litre measure.

s.def: An airtight vessel in which material is subjected to high temperatures in the chemical industry or as part of an industrial manufacturing process, especially during the smelting and forging of metal.
A pressure cooker.
ex: The retort is above boiling water. Beneath is a furnace. To the right a man is removing the chips from which the camphor has been extracted.

s.def: A crematory furnace.
To heat in a retort.
Alternative form of retorsion.

ety: From French retoucher.

s.def: To improve something (especially a photograph), by adding or correcting details, or by removing flaws.
To colour the roots of hair to match hair previously coloured.
To modify a flint tool by making secondary flaking along the cutting edge.
The act of retouching (in any sense).

ety: From French retracer, from Middle French retracier.

s.def: To trace (a line, etc. in drawing) again.
To go back over something, usually in an attempt at rediscovery.
ex: He retraced his steps, and found his keys where he had dropped them.

s.def: To undergo retracement.
The period when the beam of the cathode-ray tube returns to its initial horizontal position in order to start the next line of the display.
An instance of retracement.

ety: From Late Middle English retracten, retract (“to absorb, draw in”), from Latin retractus (“withdrawn”), the perfect passive participle of Latin retrahō (“to draw or pull back, withdraw; to bring back; to compel to turn back; to recall; to get back, recover; to hold back, restrain, withhold; to remove, take away; to bring to light again; (Late Latin) to delay”), from re- (prefix meaning ‘again’) + trahō (“to drag, pull; to extract, withdraw”). Doublet of retreat.

s.def: To pull (something) back or back inside.
ex: An airplane retracts its wheels for flight.
The collector shoes are automatically retracted when the electric handle is moved from "service off" to "lock off".

s.def: To avert (one's eyes or a gaze).
To pronounce (a sound, especially a vowel) farther to the back of the vocal tract.
To hold back (something); to restrain.
To draw back; to draw up; to withdraw.
ex: The bus was stuck at the stop as its wheelchair ramp wouldn’t retract after use.
Muscles retract after amputation.

s.def: An act of retracting or withdrawing (a mistake, a statement, etc.); a retraction.
A pulling back, especially (military) of an army or military troops; a pull-back, a retreat; also, a signal for this to be done.

A subgroup of a given group such that there is a surjective endomorphism from the ambient group to the subgroup which is constant on the subgroup; in this case the subgroup is a retract of the ambient group. In symbols: H in G is a retract of G if there exists a surjective homomorphism σ from G to…
The target of a retraction.
Synonym of retreat (“an act of accidentally injuring a horse's foot by incorrectly nailing it during shoeing”).

ety: From retract + -or.

s.def: A surgical instrument used to hold apart the edges of an incision or wound.
One who, or that which, retracts.
In breech-loading firearms, a device for withdrawing a cartridge shell from the barrel.
A chess puzzle in which a number of moves are retracted and the solver is challenged to reach an alternate outcome.
A bandage to protect soft parts of the body from injury by a surgical saw.
A muscle serving to draw in any part.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- English tread English retread From re- + tread (“grooves carved into the face of a tire”, noun).

s.def: To replace the traction-providing surface of a vehicle that employs tires, tracks or treads.
To renew the tread of a tyre, providing a cheaper alternative to buying a new tyre, but potentially introducing a risk of premature failure if performed improperly.
A used tire whose surface, the tread, has been replaced to extend its life and use.
A person who re-entered military service in World War II after serving in World War I.
ex: In Our War the Retreads usually slinked in over-aged, over-weight and overcautious in the face of a new generation.
They were retreads and recruits under a small cadre of Regular Army officers and noncoms.
We retreads upset everybody.

s.def: To tread again, to walk along again, to follow a path again.
A return over ground previously covered; a retraversal or repetition.
ex: But The West Side Waltz is otherwise a tedious retread of Mr. Thompson's previous effort, On Golden Pond.

ety: From Middle English retret, from Old French retrait or retret, from Latin retractus, from retraho. Doublet of retract, retrait, and ritratto.

s.def: The act of pulling back or withdrawing, as from something dangerous, or unpleasant.
ex: In a retreat he outruns any lackey.

s.def: To withdraw from a position, go back.
ex: The general refused to order his soldiers to retreat, despite being vastly outnumbered.

s.def: A peaceful, quiet place affording privacy or security.
ex: a mountain retreat
[…] he built his son a house of pleasure, on purpose to keep him out of harm's way; and spared neither art nor cost to make it a delicious retreat.
That pleasing shade they sought, a soft retreat / From sudden April showers, a shelter from the heat.

s.def: A peaceful, quiet place in which to urinate and defecate: an outhouse; a lavatory.
A period of retirement, seclusion, or solitude, especially for meditation, prayer, or study.
ex: We both need a week retreat after those two stressful years working in the city.
a Buddhist retreat
a company retreat

s.def: A signal for a military withdrawal.
A bugle call or drumbeat signaling the lowering of the flag at sunset, as on a military base.
ex: to-morrow the Royal Standard will be hoisted at Edinburgh Castle from reveille to retreat.

s.def: A military ceremony to lower the flag.
The move of a piece from a threatened position.
To shrink back due to generally warmer temperatures. (of a glacier)

ety: From Old French retranchier (“to get rid of, remove”) (modern French retrancher (“to cut out, take away; to cut off; to cut down”)), from re- (“again”) + tranchier, trenchier (“to cut”) (modern French trancher (“to slice”)); further etymology uncertain, but possibly either from Vulgar Latin *trinicāre (“cut in three parts”) (from the root trini from trēs (“three”), based on the model of duplicāre (“to double by dividing, split in two, tear”)), or from an alteration of Latin truncāre (“to maim b…

s.def: To cut down or reduce.
ex: And it would signal to a wider world that Britain is retrenching and not developing its infrastructure to enable growth.

s.def: To confine; to limit; to restrict.
To furnish with a retrenchment (a defensive work within a fortification).
ex: to retrench bastions

s.def: To abridge; to curtail.
To take up a new defensive position.
ex: We must retrench and try to hold on long enough for products in development to reach the market or we will be out of business.

s.def: To dig or redig a trench where one already exists.

ety: PIE word *tréyes From Latin retribuere (“repay”).

s.def: Punishment inflicted in the spirit of moral outrage or personal vengeance.

ety: Etymology tree English retrieve Proto-Indo-European *-dʰlom Proto-Italic *-ðlom Proto-Italic *-ðlis Latin -bilis Latin -ābilis Old French -ablebor. Middle English -able English -able English retrievable From retrieve + -able.

s.def: Capable of being retrieved or recovered.
ex: Mislaid items are retrievable from the Lost Property office.

s.def: From which recovery is possible.
ex: His mistakes are fatal; those of the Law are only temporary and retrievable.

ety: Recorded in Middle English c. 1410 as retreve (altered to retrive in the 16th century; modern form is from c. 1650), from Middle French retruev-, stem of Old French retrover (“to find again”, modern retrouver), itself from re- (“again”) + trover (“to find”), probably from Vulgar Latin *tropāre (“to compose”).

s.def: To regain or get back something.
ex: to retrieve one's character or independence; to retrieve a thrown ball
With late repentance now they would retrieve / The bodies they forsook, and wish to live.

s.def: To rescue (a creature).
To salvage something
To remedy or rectify something.
To remember or recall something.
To fetch or carry back something, especially (computing) a file or data record.
ex: to retrieve them from their cold, trivial conceits

s.def: To fetch and bring in game.
ex: The cook doesn't care what's shot, only what's actually retrieved.

s.def: To fetch and bring in game systematically.
ex: Dog breeds called 'retrievers' were selected for retrieving.

s.def: To fetch or carry back systematically, notably as a game.
ex: Most dogs love retrieving, regardless of what object is thrown.

s.def: To make a difficult but successful return of the ball.

ety: From retro- + act.

s.def: To act retrospectively or in opposition
to be retrospective.
To apply (a law) retroactively to situations that predate the enactment of the law.
ex: Sec. 4. The effectivity of this Act shall retroact to January 1, 2001.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re- Latin retrōder. English retro- Old French aucionbor. Middle English accioun English action English retroaction From retro- + action.

s.def: Any action that has an influence due to a past event
An opposing action; a reaction

ety: Etymology tree English retroactive Middle English -ly English -ly English retroactively From retroactive + -ly.

s.def: Done after the fact; applying to events that have previously transpired.
ex: The new legislature passed a resolution retroactively legalizing the actions of the revolutionaries that brought them to power.

ety: Ultimately from Latin retrōcēdere, from retrō- (“back, backward”) + cēdere (“to go, go back, give, return, etc.”). Equivalent to retro- + cede.

s.def: To grant back.
ex: to retrocede a territory to a former proprietor

s.def: To go back.
ex: Hospitals retrenched in the '30s while the general practitioners retroceded into a bygone era.

ety: Compare French rétrocession. See retrocede.

s.def: The transfer of risk from one reinsurer to another.
The return of land, rights, etc. previously ceded.
Metastasis of an eruption or tumour from the surface to the interior of the body.
The act of retroceding; a going back.

ety: The verb is derived from retro- (prefix meaning ‘back; backward’) + fit (“to equip, supply”). The noun, which is first attested later than the verb, is either derived: * from the verb (see above); or * from retro- + fit (“act of fitting; conformity of elements one to another”).

s.def: An act of supplying a device, structure, etc., with new components or parts that were not previously available or installed; a retrofitting.
A change made to a device, structure, etc., by introducing components or parts that were not previously available or installed.

ety: The adjective is derived from Middle English retrograd, retrograde (“of a planet: appearing to move in a direction opposite to the order of the zodiac signs, retrograde; unfortunate”), from Middle French retrograde and Old French retrograde (“of a celestial object: appearing to move backwards; moving backwards; reverse; palindromic; opposed to change”) (modern French rétrograde), and from their etymon Latin retrōgradus (“of a celestial object: appearing to move backwards”) (compare Late Latin r…

s.def: Directed or moving backwards in relation to the normal or previous direction of travel; retreating.
Reverting to an inferior or less developed state; declining, regressing.
Of the order of something: inverse, reverse.
Of ideas or a person: opposing social reform, favouring the maintenance of the status quo; conservative.
ex: retrograde ideas, morals, etc.
Such retrograde people still exist, resisting modernity, dragging their feet.

s.def: Involving a return to or a retracing of a previous course of travel.
Counterproductive to a desired outcome; contradictory, contrary.
ex: In going back to school in Wittenberg, / It is most retrograde to our desire: / And we beseech you, bend you to remain

s.def: Of a celestial body orbiting another: in the opposite direction to the orbited body's spin.
Of a celestial body: seeming to move across the sky in the opposite direction from its ordinary movement.
ex: Mercury retrograde
The inauspicious connotations of Mercury retrograde are actually quite old, evidenced in an ancient branch of astrology known as horary astrology.

s.def: Of a metamorphic change: resulting from a decrease in pressure or temperature.
Of amnesia: relating to the period leading up to the episode which caused it.

ety: From Latin retrōgressus, perfect active participle of retrōgradior (“retrograde”).

s.def: To return to an earlier, simpler or worse condition; to regress.
To go backwards; to retreat.
To return to bad behaviour; to relapse.
A retrogression.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re- Latin retrōder. English retro- Old Italian rocchetto Italian rocchettabor. English rocket English retrorocket From retro- + rocket.

s.def: A small rocket engine on a larger rocket or spacecraft, designed to slow or reverse its motion.

ety: From Latin retrorsus, contracted form of retroversus, from retro (“back”) + versum (“turned”). Doublet of retroverse.

s.def: Curved, pointed or oriented backward or downward.

ety: Borrowed from Latin retrōspectum, from retrōspicio (“to look back at”), equivalent to retro- + -spect. Compare review.

s.def: Consideration of past times.
To look or refer back to; to reflect on.
ex: To give a correct idea of the circumstances which have gradually produced this conviction, it may be useful to retrospect to an early period.

s.def: The deliberate recall of past events.
ex: "And then?" prompted Carrados, for Nora seemed to be in danger of losing herself in retrospection. "Something definite happened?"

ety: From retrospect + -ive. From Latin retrōspectus, perfect passive participle of retrōspiciō (“to look back at”).

s.def: Of, relating to, or contemplating the past.
Looking backwards.
Affecting or influencing past things; retroactive.
An exhibition of works from an extended period of an artist's activity.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re- French re- French trousser French retroussébor. English retroussé From French retroussé, past participle of retrousser (“to hitch up, hike up”), from re- (from Latin re- (“back, backwards; again”), from Proto-Italic *wre- (“again”)) + trousser (“to fold up, hitch up”).

s.def: Turned up, especially when describing the nose.
ex: You know, a touch of character – slightly retroussé nose, big mouth, perhaps a couple of freckles.
Luminous silver gray eyes outlined in sooty lashes; a pert retroussé nose and faintly carmine tinted lips, slightly full, finished the oval face.
She shares with this woman the same retroussé nose and half-moon eyes, the same asymmetrical smile.

ety: From retro- + -version.

s.def: A turning or falling back.
A backward-tilting of an anatomical strucure (e.g. the uterus).

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- English try English retry From re- + try.

s.def: To try or attempt again.
ex: to retry connecting to the Internet after an error
On October 20, Forsen streamed on Twitch as he retried to defeat the Ender Dragon as fast as he could.
There’s a chance the error code appeared as a mistake, so retrying could help you get back to the fight in no time.

s.def: To try judicially a second time.
ex: to retry a case
to retry an accused person

s.def: Another attempt.

ety: From Middle English returnen, retornen, from Anglo-Norman returner, from Old French retourner, retorner, from Medieval Latin retornare (“to turn back”), from re- + tornare (“to turn”). By surface analysis, re- + turn. Compare beturn. Displaced native Old English eftċierran, literally "eft-char".

s.def: To come or go back (to a place or person).
ex: Although the birds fly north for the summer, they return here in winter.
“I came through and I shall return,” General MacArthur declared when he spoke at Terowie of the beleagured Philippines.

s.def: To go back in thought, narration, or argument.
ex: To return to my story[…]

s.def: To turn back, retreat.
ex: ‘I suppose here is none woll be glad to returne – and as for me,’ seyde Sir Cador, ‘I had lever dye this day that onys to turne my bak.’

s.def: To turn (something) round.
ex: Whan Kyng Marke harde hym sey that worde, he returned his horse and abode by hym.

s.def: To give something back to its original holder or owner.
ex: You should return the library book within one month.

s.def: To recur; to come again.
ex: Winter returns every year.

s.def: To place or put back something where it had been.
ex: Please return your hands to your lap.
Strain the stock and return it to the pan.

s.def: To give in requital or recompense; to requite.
To reciprocate (a visit or telephone call, electronic message, etc.).
ex: Hello, I’m just returning your call. What did you want to talk about?
I wrote to my ex-wife but she won't return my emails.

s.def: To take back something to a vendor for a complete or partial refund.
Having a rounded apex with a small central notch.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- English unification English reunification From re- + unification.

s.def: The unification of something that was previously divided; used especially of a country.
ex: Many of Spenser's readers today find the cleavings and reunifications of Redcrosse and Una presenting a psychodrama of mental fragmentation […]

ety: From Middle French reunion (modern French réunion). By surface analysis, re- + union. Doublet of Réunion.

s.def: The process or act of reuniting.
ex: The reunion took forever, but it was worth it.
It was a tearful and heartfelt reunion as the trapped miners finally saw their dear loved ones again.

s.def: A planned event at which members of a dispersed group meet together.
ex: Are you going to the high-school reunion this year?

s.def: To form a reunion or an act of reuniting.

ety: Abbreviation of revolutions, rpm

s.def: To increase the speed of a motor, or to operate at a higher speed.
ex: He revved the engine in a rather macho style.
You could hear the engines revving from a mile away.
Two in a row, everybody knows at the green light you rev it on the red line.

s.def: Clipping of revolution (of something spinning).
ex: Up came the revs again, slam the door shut, kick the stick off the throttle and up through the gears, down the others side! Whee! Made it again!

s.def: Clipping of revenue
Clipping of reverend

ety: The verb is derived from re- (prefix meaning ‘again, anew’) + vamp (“to patch, repair, or refurbish”). The noun is derived from the verb.

s.def: To improve, renew, renovate, or revise (something).
ex: They plan to revamp the historical theater in the old downtown.
"We'll work on revamping our strategy in the morning," I say, "Now I think we all need some sleep. It's been a long night."

s.def: An act of improving, renewing, renovating, or revising something; an improvement, renovation, revamping, or revision.
ex: a revamp of a website
The following appear rather like revamps of old versions absolutely than absolutely new jokes: […]
Work on the Grade 1-listed building starts early next year, with LMJV (Lang O'Rourke and J. Murphy & Sons) to carry out the revamp.

ety: From the French revanche (“revenge”) + -ism, based on revanchisme. By surface analysis, revanche + -ism. Piecewise doublet of revengism.

s.def: The political policy of endeavouring to regain lost territory.

An imitation of a rose made of ribbon or other material, worn as an ornament or symbol, especially:
A decorative inlay surrounding the sound hole of a guitar.
A red color.
A rose burner.
One or more whorls of leaves, clustered tightly at the base of a plant.
A plant growth form in which the plant grows outward in all directions for a short distance, producing a small round shape.
Any structure having a flowerlike form; especially, the group of five broad ambulacra on the upper side of the spatangoid and clypeastroid sea urchins.
A flowerlike color marking, as on the leopard.
A floral pattern in latte art.

ety: From rose + water.

s.def: A liquid produced by steeping rose petals in water, used as a coloring agent and a flavoring ingredient in certain foods.

ety: A compound of rose + wood, originally so named because of the rose-scented aromatic oil derived from it; applied in later senses on account of these woods’ predominantly reddish-brown colour.

s.def: The fragrant wood of Dalbergia nigra, a Brazilian tree in the legume family, which has a sweet smell.
Any of several dozen woods, resembling that of Dalbergia nigra in some respect.
The wood of a South American tree, Aniba rosaeodora, in the laurel family, with fragrant wood from which an essential oil is distilled.
Wood and plant of Pterocarpus spp., for example African rosewood or mukula or Burmese rosewood (Pterocarpus indicus, syn. Pterocarpus santalinus).

ety: From Old French raisine, rousine, variants of résine. Doublet of resin.

s.def: Resin.
ex: ‘It is delicate,’ said Pansa, ‘but there is perhaps the least particle too much of rosin in its flavor.’
A thick, fat smoke oozed out from the fire, and a heavy smell of burned rosin and singed hair filled the air.

s.def: A solid form of resin, obtained from liquid resin by vaporizing its volatile components.
To apply rosin to (something); to rub or cover with rosin.
ex: We waited expectantly as the guest violinist rosined his bow in preparation for playing.
The devil opened up his case and he said, "I'll start this show." And fire flew from his fingertips as he rosined up his bow.

ety: Borrowed from Dutch rooster (“gridiron, table, list”), from Middle Dutch roosten (“to roast”). More at roast.

s.def: A list of individuals or groups, usually for an organization of some kind such as military officers and enlisted personnel enrolled in a particular unit; a muster roll; a sports team, with the names of players who are eligible to be placed in the lineup for a particular game; or a list of students…
ex: I'm number 12 on the roster for tonight's game.

s.def: A list of the jobs to be performed by members of an organization and often with the date and time that they are expected to perform them.
ex: The secretary has produced a new cleaning roster for the Church over the remainder of the year.

s.def: A schedule or timetable setting out shift times and dates for each employee of a business.
ex: Before uni starts check your work roster with your uni schedule to make sure there are no clashes with your classes.

s.def: A bracketed list that shows the elements of a set.
To place the name of (a person) on a roster.
ex: I have rostered you for cleaning duties on the first Monday of each month.
New York Central rostered literally hundreds of engine subclassifications in contrast to the Spartan simplicity of Pennsy's ranks.

s.def: To show the elements of a set by listing them inside brackets.
plural of rostrum

ety: From Latin rostrum.

s.def: Relating to the rostrum.
Serving as a rostrum.
ex: rostral column

s.def: A scale in reptiles on the median plate of the tip of the snout that borders the mouth opening.

ety: Learned borrowing from Latin rōstrum (“beak, snout”), from rōd(ō) (“gnaw”) + -trum, from Proto-Indo-European *Hreh₃d- + *-trom. The pulpit sense is a back-formation from the name of the Roman Rōstra, the platforms in the Forum where politicians made speeches. The Rōstra were decorated with (and named for) the beaks (prows) of ships from naval victories.

s.def: A dais, pulpit, or similar platform for a speaker, conductor, or other performer.
ex: He saw a crowd listening to a man who was talking from the rostrum of a kitchen-chair.

s.def: A platform for a film or television camera.
The projecting prow of a rowed warship, such as a trireme.
The beak.
The beak-shaped projection on the head of insects such as weevils.
The snout of a dolphin.
The oral or nasal region of a human used for anatomical location (i.e. rostral).
Any beak-like extension.
The inner segment of the coronal lobes in asclepiads.

ety: From Middle English rosy; equivalent to rose + -y.

s.def: Rose-coloured.
ex: Near-synonyms: rosish, rubicund

s.def: Of any reddish hue from bright pink to the color of ruddy cheeks in a light-skinned person.
ex: If I close my eyes I can see Marie today as I saw her then. Round, rosy face, snub nose, dark hair piled up in a chignon.

s.def: Otherwise resembling a rose, as for example in scent of perfume.
Optimistic.
To make pinkish in colour.
ex: Two flags of color rosied the jut of his cheekbones, giving him an unexpectedly boyish look.

s.def: To present in a deceptively optimistic or positive light.
Alternative spelling of Rosie (“tea”).
ex: I fancy a cup of rosy.

der: everything in the garden is rosy
everything is rosy in the garden

ety: Inherited from Middle English roten, rotten, from Old English rotian (“to rot, become corrupted, ulcerate, putrefy”), from Proto-West Germanic *rotēn, from Proto-Germanic *rutāną (“to rot”).

s.def: To suffer decomposition due to biological action, especially by fungi or bacteria.
ex: The apple left in the cupboard all that time had started to rot.
Fix'd like a plant on his peculiar spot, / To draw nutrition, propagate, and rot.

s.def: The process of becoming rotten; putrefaction.
To decline in function or utility.
ex: Your brain will rot if you spend so much time on the computer, Tony!

s.def: To (cause to) deteriorate in any way, as in morals; to corrupt.
To make putrid; to cause to be wholly or partially decomposed by natural processes.
ex: to rot vegetable fiber

s.def: To spend a long period of time (in an unpleasant place or state).
ex: to rot in prison
to rot in Hell
If I hadn't rotted in bed all day I would've come...

s.def: To expose, as flax, to a process of maceration, etc., for the purpose of separating the fiber; to ret.
To talk nonsense.
ex: “Did they hang you well?” said Porson. “Don’t rot,” said Mr Watkins; “I don’t like it.”

s.def: Damn; blast.
Decaying matter.
ex: When a turkey vulture detects the scent of rot, it circles down, tracing the plume of chemicals to its source.

ety: Borrowed from Latin rota (“wheel”). Doublet of rotor and ruote.

s.def: A schedule that allocates some task, responsibility or (rarely) privilege between a set of people according to a (possibly periodic) calendar.
ex: on a rota basis

s.def: A kind of zither used in the Middle Ages in church music.
ex: Along the creek bed he came, plucking a rota, a zither of five strings with bone-yoke facings and a beaverskin carrying-bag thrown over his shoulder.

ety: Etymology tree English rotary Proto-Indo-European *-nós Proto-Italic *-nos Proto-Italic *-ānos Latin -ānus Old French -ainder. Middle English -an English -an English Rotarian From rotary + -an.

s.def: A member of a Rotary Club.

ety: Attested mid 18th century, from Medieval Latin rotarius, from Latin rota (“wheel”).

s.def: Capable of rotation.
ex: A rotary engine revolves the heads rather than having pistons go back and forth.

s.def: Any of the clubs making up the international Rotary International movement for community service.
A roundabout, traffic circle.

ety: Borrowed from Latin rotātus, perfect passive participle of rotō (“revolve”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from rota (“wheel”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix).

s.def: To spin, turn, or revolve.
ex: He rotated in his chair to face me.
The earth rotates.

s.def: To advance through a sequence; to take turns.
ex: The nurses' shifts rotate each week.

s.def: To lift the nose during takeoff, just prior to liftoff.
ex: The aircraft rotates at sixty knots.

s.def: To spin, turn, or revolve something.
ex: Rotate the dial to the left.

s.def: To advance something through a sequence; to allocate or deploy in turns.
To replace older materials or to place older materials in front of newer ones so that older ones get used first.
ex: The supermarket rotates the stock daily so that old foods don't sit around.

s.def: To grow or plant (crops) in a certain order.
Having the parts spreading out like a wheel; wheel-shaped.
ex: a rotate spicule or scale; a rotate corolla

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *Hreth₂- Proto-Indo-European *Hróth₂eh₂der. Proto-Italic *rotā Latin rota Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ Proto-Indo-European *-éh₂ Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-eh₂yéti Proto-Indo-European *-h₂tiinflu. Proto-Italic *-ājō Proto-Italic *-āō Latin -ō Latin rotō Proto-Indo-European *-tis Proto-Indo-European *-Hō Proto-Indo-European *-tiHō Proto-Italic *-tiō Latin -tiō Latin rotātiōbor. English rotation Borrowed from Latin rotātiō. By surface analysis,…

s.def: The act of turning around a centre or an axis.
ex: The earth's rotation about its axis is responsible for its being slightly oblate rather than a sphere.

s.def: A single complete cycle around a centre or an axis.
ex: Earth's moon completes a rotation every twenty-seven days or so.

s.def: A regular variation in a sequence, such as to even out wear, or people taking turns in a task; a duty roster.
ex: Applying crop rotation to a field avoids depleting soil nutrients the way repeated use of a single crop might do.
In rotation, each member of the group would be responsible for the beacon fire.
The medical resident finished a two-week rotation in pediatrics and began one in orthopaedics.

s.def: Тhe movement of investments between different sectors of an economy, or styles of investing, based on anticipated changes in the economic or market cycle.
An operation on a metric space that is a continuous isometry and fixes at least one point.
ex: The function mapping (x,y) to (−y,x) is a rotation.

s.def: The set of starting pitchers of a team.
The step during takeoff when the pilot commands the vehicle to lift the nose wheel off the ground during the takeoff roll. (see also: V2)
Repeated play of songs on a radio station, advertisements on a television channel, etc.
ex: The new single enjoyed heavy rotation on MTV.

ety: From rotate + -or.

s.def: One who or that which rotates.
A muscle by which a joint can be rotated.
A revolving reverberatory furnace.
A banner ad that cycles through multiple advertisements.
A set of four smaller muscles in the shoulder responsible for rotating the humerus (upper arm bone).

ety: From Middle English rote (“custom, habit, wont, condition, state”), further origin unknown. Found in the Middle English phrase bi rote (“by heart, according to form, expertly”), c. 1300. Some have proposed a relationship either with Old French rote/rute (“route”), or Latin rota (“wheel”) (see rotary), but the OED calls both suggestions groundless. Another explanation might be the metaphorical comparison between anything repetitive and playing the rote.

s.def: Mechanical routine; a fixed, habitual, repetitive, or mechanical course of procedure.
ex: The pastoral scenes from those commercials don’t bear too much resemblance to the rote of daily life on a farm.
He could perform by rote any of his roles in Shakespeare.

s.def: By repetition or practice and without much thought.
ex: The former may be seen as a more rote form of learning, contrasting with the latter which appears to include "executive" aspects

s.def: To go out by rotation or succession; to rotate.
To learn or repeat by rote.
The roar of the surf; the sound of waves breaking on the shore.
A kind of guitar, the notes of which were produced by a small wheel or wheel-like arrangement; an instrument similar to the hurdy-gurdy.
ex: extracting mistuned dirges from their harps, crowds, and rotes

s.def: Synonym of crowd.

ety: From rot + gut.

s.def: Raw or poor-quality alcoholic liquor.
ex: Near-synonym: red-eye
His mother, Dorothy, hung around longer, long enough for her to choke on her own vomit. She had that taste—rotgut, the rougher the better.

ety: From Latin rota (“wheel”) + -fer (“-bearing”), after Italian rotifero.

s.def: Any of many minute aquatic multicellular organisms, of the phylum Rotifera, that have a ring of cilia resembling a wheel.

ety: From French rôtisserie, from rôtir ‘to roast’. Doublet of rosticceria and roastery.

s.def: A cooking device with which food is roasted on a rotating spit.
ex: There will be no more misery / When the world is our rotisserie
Rotisseries are essentially self-basting because most of the juices stay on the meat and distribute across it while the rotisserie is being turned.
Rotisseries cook with dry heat, but the continual rotation of foods as they cook helps maintain their natural juices.

s.def: A shop or restaurant selling food cooked in this manner.
ex: Restaurants, chop-houses, rotisseries, abound in every part^([of San Francisco]).
We refuse to be drawn into the debate over which of St. Barts' two rotisseries is the best. They're both good.

s.def: Ellipsis of rotisserie baseball, synonym of fantasy baseball.
Ellipsis of rotisserie sports, synonym of fantasy sports.
To cook on a rotisserie.

ety: From German Rotogravur, derived from the Berlin printing firm Rotogravur Deutsche Tiefdruck Gesellschaft, the name of which is conjectured to be a portmanteau of Rotophot and Deutsche Photogravur.

s.def: A printing process by which the paper is rolled through intaglio cylinders.
A print made by such a method.
ex: On the avenue, Fifth Avenue, the photographers will snap us, And you'll find that you're in the rotogravure.
On the desk before her lay the rotogravure section of the Sunday Chronicle.

ety: From an irregular clipping of rotator, originally in mathematics, coined by English mathematician and philosopher William Kingdon Clifford based on vector, see quotations. Doublet of rota and ruote.

s.def: A type of powerful horizontal-axis atmospheric vortex generated by the interaction of strong winds with mountainous terrain.
The set of cells within an oscillator that switch between being alive and dead over the course of the oscillator's period.
A rotating part of a mechanical device; for example, in an electric motor, generator, alternator, or pump.
A quantity having magnitude, direction, and position.

An amusement park and carnival ride consisting of a rotating cylindrical chamber in which centrifugal force adheres riders to the wall as the floor drops away, creating a sensation of defying gravity.

ety: From rotor + craft.

s.def: Any aircraft that obtains its lift from rotors (usually either a helicopter or an aerial drone with rotors).

ety: From Middle English roten, from Old Norse rotinn (“decayed, rotten”), past participle of an unrecorded verb related to Old Norse rotna (“to rot”) and Old English rotian (“to rot”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *rutāną (“to rot”). See rot. By surface analysis, rot + -en (past participle).

s.def: In a state of decay.
ex: The floors were damaged and the walls were rotten.
His mouth stank and his teeth were rotten.

s.def: Of perishable items, overridden with bacteria and other infectious agents.
ex: If you leave a bin unattended for a few weeks, the rubbish inside will turn rotten.

s.def: Cruel, mean or immoral.
ex: That man is a rotten father.
This rotten policy will create more injustice in this country.
Something is rotten in the State of Denmarke.

s.def: Bad or terrible.
ex: Why is the weather always rotten in this city?
It was a rotten idea to take the boat out today.
She has the flu and feels rotten.

s.def: Of stone or rock, crumbling or friable; in a loose or disintegrated state.
Very drunk, intoxicated.
To an extreme degree.
ex: That kid is spoilt rotten.
The girls fancy him something rotten.
"It's old man Challenger's show and we are here by his good will, so it would be rotten bad form if we didn't follow his instructions to the letter."

ety: From rotten + stone.

s.def: A soft, friable limestone, used in polishes.
To polish with rottenstone.

ety: From rot + -er.

s.def: A despicable, worthless person; a scoundrel.
ex: Some Johnny with brains produces a hypothesis. Everybody calls him a rotter at first. But he remains calm in the face of opprobrium.

ety: Borrowed from Dutch Rotterdam.

s.def: A city in South Holland, Netherlands.
A municipality of South Holland, Netherlands.

ety: From Arabic رُطْل (ruṭl), variant of classical رِطْل (riṭl) and vernacular رَطْل (raṭl), under the influence of French rotte and Italian rotolo, ultimately from Ancient Greek λίτρα (lítra). Doublet of arratel, libbra, Libra, libra, lira, litra, litre, and livre.

s.def: A former Middle Eastern and North African unit of dry weight, usually between 1–5 pounds (0.5–2.5 kg).

ety: Learned borrowing from Latin rotundus (“round”), from Latin rota (“wheel”), from Proto-Indo-European *Hreth₂- (“to run, to roll”). Doublet of round.

s.def: Having a round, spherical or curved shape; circular; orbicular.
Having a round body shape; portly or pudgy; obese.
Full and rich; orotund; sonorous; full-toned.

ety: Learned borrowing from Latin rotunda, from rotundus (“round”). In the architectural sense, from Sancta Maria Rotunda (the name for a church in the Pantheon).

s.def: A round building, usually small, often with a dome.
A Gothic typeface used in early printed books in Northern Italy, based on a rounded script developed in the 13th cent.; the manuscript hand on which this typeface was based.
Alternative spelling of rotonda.
ex: TPLEX Rotunda is a roundabout located in Rosario, La Union.

s.def: A form of cupola that has pentagons rather than squares or rectangles.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French roturier.

s.def: A commoner or plebeian; a person of low rank; especially, in pre-Revolutionary France, a member of the social class comprising all who were not nobles or clergy.
Alternative spelling of roué.

ety: Borrowed from French Rouen, from Latin Rotomagus. Replaced Middle English Rone, from Anglo-Norman Ron.

s.def: The prefecture of the department of Seine-Maritime, and the capital of the region of Normandy, France, on the Seine River.

ety: Borrowed from French rouge, from Latin rubeus. Compare rare Middle English rouge, rouȝ (“red”); later borrowed again, as it is not attested until c. 1750. The game senses are of unknown origin according to the Oxford English Dictionary.

s.def: Of a reddish pink colour.
Any reddish pink colour.

A single point awarded when a team kicks the ball out of its opponent's end zone, or when a kicked ball becomes dead within the non-kicking team's end zone. Etymology uncertain; it is thought that in the early years of the sport, a red flag indicated that a single had been scored.
In the Eton wall game, a scrummage, melée.

In the Eton College field game, a scoring move accomplished by touching the ball down behind the opponents' goal-line (somewhat similar to the try in rugby). Originally, the player who scored the rouge had a chance to kick a goal, and the rouge was used as a tie-breaker if an equal number of goals…
ex: The 7 got 1 "gaol" and 1 "ruge"; the 11 got 1 "gaol" and 4 "ruges"
A rouge is obtained by touching the ball first, after it has been kicked behind

s.def: From 1862 to 1868, a similar scoring move in Sheffield rules football. From 1862 to 1867, accomplished by touching the ball down after it had been kicked between two "rouge flags" either side of the goal. From 1867-1868, awarded for kicking the ball between the rouge flags and under the crossbar.
ex: A rouge is obtained by the player who first touches the ball after it has been kicked between the rouge flags

s.def: A red amorphous powder consisting of ferric oxide, used in polishing and as a cosmetic; crocus; jeweller's rouge.
Red or pink makeup to add colour to the cheeks; blusher.
To apply rouge (makeup).
ex: She rouged her face before setting out for the party.

ety: From Middle English rough, roughe, roȝe, row, rou, ru, ruȝ, ruh, from Old English rūg, rūh, from Proto-Germanic *rūhaz. Cognate with Scots ruch, rouch (“rough”), Saterland Frisian ruuch, rouch (“rough”), West Frisian rûch (“rough”), Low German ruuch (“rough”), Dutch ruig (“rough”), German rau(h) (“rough”), Danish ru (“uneven on the surface, "rough", "rugged"”).

s.def: Not smooth; uneven.
ex: rough surface

s.def: Approximate; hasty or careless; not finished.
ex: a rough copy
a rough estimate
a rough guess

s.def: Turbulent.
ex: rough weather

s.def: Difficult; trying.
ex: Being a teenager nowadays can be rough.

s.def: Crude; unrefined.
ex: His manners are a bit rough, but he means well.

s.def: Worn; shabby; weather-beaten.
ex: "You find us a bit rough," apologized the young man, with something of contempt towards his surroundings. "We weren't expecting visitors."

s.def: Having socio-economic problems, hence possibly dangerous.
ex: the rough bit of town

s.def: Violent; not careful or subtle.
ex: This box has been through some rough handling.

s.def: Loud and hoarse; offensive to the ear; harsh; grating.
ex: a rough tone
a rough voice
But most by Numbers judge a Poet's song, / And smooth or rough, with them

s.def: Not polished; uncut.
ex: a rough diamond

der: have a rough time of it

s.def: Alternative spelling of rough and ready.

ety: From rough + and + tumble.

s.def: Active, vigorous and rough, with the possibility of harm.
ex: An assistant about the theatre grappled him, and they were soon upon the floor engaged in a regular rough-and-tumble fight.

s.def: Highly competitive.
ex: She found fame and success in the rough-and-tumble garment district.

s.def: An environment of rough activity.
A person who characteristically engages in such activity.
ex: This will appear a very tedious process to some of our rough-and-tumbles.

s.def: Rough activity; fighting or brawling; a fight.
ex: "You played Rugger for Ireland, did you not? You don't mind a possible rough-and-tumble, do you?" Malone grinned over the receiver.
She liked ragging; but ragging — and nothing more — these rough-and-tumbles remained
As for rough-and-tumbles, the Quaker saw no hope of suppressing them. Few nights passed without such fights […]

s.def: To engage in rough-and-tumble activity.
ex: But, for all that, our British experience of electioneering "rough-and-tumbling'" has long blunted the edge of our moral anger.
Although examples could be found throughout the South, rough-and-tumbling was best suited to the backwoods.

ety: From rough-legged + buzzard.

s.def: Buteo lagopus, a medium-large bird of prey.

ety: From rough (“not smooth; crude, unrefined”) + -age (suffix forming nouns with the sense of appurtenance or collection).

s.def: Originally (archaic), garbage, rubbish, or waste; later (agriculture) the portions of a crop which are discarded, such as husks, stalks, etc.; also, agricultural waste such as weeds.
Coarse or rough plant material such as hay and silage used as animal fodder.

Substances, generally of plant origin, consisting mostly of complex carbohydrates which are undigested when eaten by humans, and which therefore help the passage of food and waste through the alimentary tract; dietary fibre.
ex: I keep telling her not to eat all that roughage for brekky; prunes, bran, and baked beans.

ety: From rough + cast.

s.def: A crude model.
ex: The whole piece […]seems […]a loose model and roughcast of what I design to do.
All the objects left in or near the quarries are unfinished roughcasts.
They first attached the paper-cuttings directly onto the roughcast of china, then they applied glaze to it.

s.def: A rough surface finish, as of a plaster or stucco wall.
A mixture of pebbles or similar material used to finish a plaster or concrete wall.
To shape crudely; to form in its first rudiments, without correction or polish.
ex: This rough cast unhewn poetry was instead of stage plays for 120 years
Dutt (1913) states that madraspatanum wasps build all their cells and then roughcast the whole group together, i.e. that they make a crepissage.

s.def: To apply a roughcast finish to.
ex: to roughcast a wall or building

s.def: Unpolished.
ex: A brilliant blaze, kindled with dry wood, enlightened the whole interior of this fresh looking, roughcast, timbered apartment.
Understand: I'm a roughcast fly fisherman, an empirical self-taught duffer.

ety: From rough + dry.

s.def: In laundry work, to dry without smoothing or ironing.
ex: Mr. Seeders was thin and had light hair, and appeared to have been recently roughdried and starched.
This includes looading, unloading, and operating controls of machines to wash, dye, starch, roughdry, or condition items for pressing.

s.def: To dry shaped bricks before they are fired in a kiln.
ex: He had a cough which spoke sometimes of roughdried bricks in a builder's yard, and his calf muscles spoiled the particoloured set of his stockings.

s.def: Having been dried but not ironed.
Having been been sawn, edged, trimmed, and dried, but not surfaced or dressed by planing.
ex: The dry lumber was pulled from the kiln and held in the roughdry shed for a day or two before unstacking.

ety: From rough + -en.

s.def: To make rough.
ex: The wind began to roughen the surface of the sea.
They roughened the edges of the stone to give it a rustic look.

s.def: To become rough.
Alternative form of rough-hew.

ety: From rough + house.

s.def: Of behavior, rowdy, boisterous, or fighting.
ex: The film presents Gia as a roughhouse girl plopped down in the world of instant fame, sex, money, and drugs.

s.def: Rowdy behavior.
To behave rowdily or violently.
ex: Out in the street, some delinquents were roughhousing, until the police drove by.

s.def: To treat (someone or something) roughly or violently.
ex: Out in the street, some delinquents were roughhousing a victim, until the police drove by.

ety: Etymology tree English rough Proto-Indo-European *leyg-der. Proto-Germanic *līkąder. Proto-Germanic *-līkaz Proto-Germanic *-ê Proto-Germanic *-līkê Proto-West Germanic *-līkē Old English -līċe Middle English -ly English -ly English roughly From rough + -ly.

s.def: In a rough manner; without kindness, softness, or gentleness.
ex: They treated the prisoners roughly [...] slashing pitilessly with their whips to drive them as wretched animals before them.

s.def: Unevenly or irregularly.
Without precision or exactness; imprecisely but close to in quantity or amount; approximately.
ex: Satanism can be divided, roughly, into two branches: the Luciferians and the Palladists.

ety: From rough + rider.

s.def: A horsebreaker.
A noncommissioned officer in the British cavalry whose duty is to assist the riding master.
A member of the 1st United States Volunteer Cavalry during the Spanish-American War

ety: From rough + shod.

s.def: Of a horse: having hooves shod with horseshoes that have calks or projecting parts to prevent slipping.
Brutal or domineering.
ex: In the roughshod horny world of boys, I had studied my companions closely to make sure that I wasn't being too "queer" for them.

ety: From French roulade, from rouler (“to roll”), from Old French roler.

s.def: An elaborate embellishment of several notes sung to one syllable.
ex: He heard only here and there the ecstatic burst of a mocking-bird's wonderful roulades.

s.def: A slice of meat that is rolled up, stuffed, and cooked.
To sing an elaborate embellishment of several notes to one syllable.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *Hreth₂- Proto-Indo-European *Hróth₂eh₂der. Proto-Italic *rotā Latin rota Proto-Indo-European *-lós Proto-Indo-European *-elós Proto-Italic *-elos Latin -ulus Latin rotulader. Latin rotulāre Old French roeler French rouler ▲ Proto-Italic *-elos Latin -lus Latin -ellus Old French -el Middle French -eau French -eau French rouleaubor. English rouleau Borrowed from French rouleau.

s.def: A little roll; a roll of coins put up in paper, or something resembling such a roll.
ex: We always judge of others by ourselves; and his idea of Cupid's quiver is a rouleau.
Early in the morning, the rouleau of gold was left at my door in a little box, with my name on the outside.
[…] he liked your philosophy, and hopes you'll accept of this, which from its weight I take to be a little rouleau of guineas.

s.def: A decorative technique that involves creating patterns with piping, cording or bias tape. A rouleau loop uses the same cord or piping as a way of fastening buttons, most notably down the back of bridal gowns.
ex: rouleau turner
rouleau loop

s.def: A stack of aggregated red blood cells, as seen in certain haematological and other diseases.
One of a bundle of fascines to cover besiegers.

ety: Borrowed from French roulette (“roulette, little wheel”). The sense "situation with a random chance of incurring serious harm" may be abstracted from Russian roulette.

s.def: A game of chance in which a small ball is made to move round rapidly on a circle divided off into numbered (usually red and black) spaces. When the ball stops, it indicates the result of a variety of wagers permitted by the game.
An instance of risk-taking, especially when the downside exceeds the upside (contrary to the game of roulette where only the wager is lost).
ex: They would all rather take their chances with the existing policy-making roulette rather than follow process discipline.
By contrast giving treatments open-label slows everything down by leading us up blind alleys while playing roulette with our patients' lives.

s.def: A small toothed wheel used by engravers to roll over a plate in order to produce rows of dots.
A similar wheel used to roughen the surface of a plate, as in making alterations in a mezzotint.
The locus of a point on a plane curve that rolls without slipping along another fixed plane curve.
Any of the small incisions on a sheet of stamps, used as an alternative to perforations.
A cylindrical curler for the hair.
To separate or decorate by incisions made with a small toothed wheel.
ex: to roulette a sheet of postage stamps

ety: From Middle English round, rounde, from Old Northern French roünt, rund, Old French ront, runt, reont ( > French rond), from both Late Latin retundus and the original Latin rotundus. The noun developed partly from the adjective and partly from the corresponding French noun rond. Doublet of rotund.

s.def: Of shape:
ex: We sat at a round table to make conversation easier.

s.def: Complete, whole, not lacking.
ex: The baker sold us a round dozen.

s.def: Pronounced with the lips drawn together; rounded.
ex: "Supposing somebody sees you, with all those flowers too? Supposing somebody writes him a letter? Ooooh!" (a pure round open Tamil O.)

s.def: A circular or spherical object or part of an object.
ex: in labyrinth of many a round self-rolled
All at once the sun was through, a round of dulled silver, racing slantwise through the clouds yet always staying in the same place.

s.def: One of the specified pre-determined segments of the total time of a sport event, such as a boxing or wrestling match, during which contestants compete before being signaled to stop.
A stage, level, set of events in a game
ex: qualifying rounds of the championship

s.def: The hindquarters of a bovine; a round of beef.
individual ammunition shell
card games: moment from the deal until the players are finished with the cards
Convenient for rounding other numbers to; for example, ending in a zero.
ex: One hundred is a nice round number.

ety: From Middle English rounde table, ronde tabell, equivalent to round + table.

s.def: A conference at which participants of similar status discuss and exchange views.
A television show segment in which pundits or reporters discuss current events.
Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see round, table.

ety: From round (“complete, entire"; "forming a circle or cycle”) + trip (“journey”).

s.def: A trip from one destination to another and then returning to the starting location.
ex: Margaret purchased a single round trip ticket to and from Chicago, as it was cheaper than buying two one-way tickets.

s.def: In an oil-drilling operation, the raising, disassembly and replacement of the drilling equipment.
A form of barter that involves the sale of an unused asset and the purchase of the same asset back again, or a similar one, typically used in accounting fraud.
The investment of a borrowed overdraft in order to make a profit in the same market.
The export and eventual reimport of a file, data, etc. without loss of fidelity.
Having a rounded upper back, and shoulders that bend forward.
Continuous; incessant; without interruption; all day long, 24 hours per day; nonstop: from the concept that it happens while the hands of the clock go all the way around.
ex: They are protected by round-the-clock guards.

ety: From round + about [from early 20th c.].

s.def: A road junction at which traffic streams circularly around a central island.
Indirect, circuitous, or circumlocutionary.
ex: [S]he fled, running like a deer, doubling and turning through alleys and back streets until by a very roundabout road she reached her own room.
Mr. Rather flew to the area in a roundabout fashion, first landing in Bahrain, from there flying to Islamabad and then heading to Kabul by land.

s.def: Encircling; enveloping; comprehensive.
A detour.
A short, close-fitting coat or jacket worn by men or boys, especially in the 19th century.
A horizontal wheel which rotates around a central axis when pushed and on which children ride, often found in parks as a children's play apparatus.
A fairground carousel.
A round dance.
To play on a roundabout (carousel)
To talk in a roundabout, indirect manner

ety: From Middle English roundel, rundel, rondel, from Old French rondel (“something round and flat”), a diminutive of rond (“round”). More at round.

s.def: Anything having a round form; a round figure; a circle.
ex: the London Underground roundel
The Overground has been given a seat at the Underground table. It has the roundel, the Johnston typeface, and it is on the Tube map.

s.def: A roundelay or rondelay.
ex: Come, now a roundel and a fairy song ... Fairies sing.

s.def: A small circular shield, sometimes not more than a foot in diameter, used by soldiers in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries.
A circular spot; a charge in the form of a small coloured circle.
A circular insignia painted on an aircraft to identify its nationality or service.
A bastion of a circular form.
An umbrella.
ex: […] a Roundel-boy; whose business, is, to walk by his master, and defend him with his Roundel or Umbrella from the heat of the sun.

ety: From Middle French rondelet, diminutive of Old French rondel (French: rondeau). Ending -lay either from lay (“ballad or sung poem”), or from virelay.

s.def: A poem or song having a line or phrase repeated at regular intervals.
ex: It fell upon a holly eve, Hey ho, hollidaye! When holly fathers wont to shrieve, Now gynneth this roundelay.

s.def: A dance in a circle.
Anything having a round form; a roundel.

ety: From Middle English rounder, roundere, equivalent to round + -er (comparative suffix).

s.def: comparative form of round: more round
A Methodist preacher traveling a circuit, also referred to as a circuit rider.
ex: My daddy was a rounder, he wore a rounder's hat and coat.

s.def: A railroad man who worked at a roundhouse, operating the turntable.
A person who earns a living by playing cards
A person who makes the rounds of bars, saloons, and similar establishments; figuratively, a debaucher or roué
One who rounds; one who comes about frequently or regularly.
ex: […] itt is order'd that 18 Souldiers, 1 Corporall & 1 Rounder goe upon the Sloop […]

s.def: A tool for making an edge or surface round.
A fight lasting a specified number of rounds.
A sports league draft selection in a specified round or the player drafted with that selection.

ety: From round + -head.

s.def: Having a dome-shaped head.
ex: The roundhead screw and its fraternal twins, the button head and pan head screws, have a head that is flat on the bottom and hemispherical on top.
You can use flat-head screws and plug the holes, or you can use roundhead blue screws and let the heads project.

s.def: A roundhead screw, one with a domed head.
Alternative letter-case form of Roundhead (“parliament supporter in the English Civil War”)
ex: You roundhead whore, sock it up, or me will kill you, begar.
He added that they 'fell upon all that have short hair' and cried out, 'A roundhead! A roundhead!'

s.def: A male whose penis is circumcised.
ex: The roundheads in the school showers easily equalled the cavaliers.

s.def: A circular platform at the end of a pier or breakwater.
Any of various agarics of the genus Stropharia.

ety: From round + house, a calque of Dutch rondhuis (“guardhouse”). First attested in the Mid-15th c.

s.def: A circular prison, especially a small local lockup or station house.
A traditional circular dwelling elevated on stilts with a conical roof found in part of Southeast Asia.
A prehistoric dwelling typical of northwest Europe in the Iron Age and Bronze Age.
The uppermost room or cabin of any note upon the stern of a ship.
A privy near the bow of a vessel, especially as reserved for officers.
A circular building in which locomotives are housed, sometimes with a turntable.
A punch or kick delivered with an exaggerated sweeping movement.
In the game of pinochle, a meld consisting of a queen and king in each of the four suits.
To punch or kick with an exaggerated sweeping movement.
ex: We focused on the nerve-agent feint, and got roundhoused by the insurgent hook.

ety: By surface analysis, round + -ing.

s.def: Round or nearly round; becoming round; roundish.
The act of making anything round, as the lips in pronouncing some vowels.
The act by which a numerical value is rounded.
The numerical value obtained by this process.
A rounded surface; a curve.
In bookbinding, the shaping of the folded and sewed sheets into a convex form at the back.

ety: Etymology tree English round Proto-Indo-European *-iskos Proto-Germanic *-iskaz Proto-West Germanic *-isk Old English -isċ Middle English -isch English -ish English roundish From round + -ish.

s.def: Somewhat round.
ex: Leaflets 9-11, roundish, of a firm texture, the lowest pair smaller than the rest, glaucous.

ety: From rounds + -man.

s.def: A worker who makes rounds, especially in order to deliver goods.
A policeman who acts as inspector.

ety: Deverbal from round up.

s.def: An activity in which cattle are herded together in order to be inspected, counted, branded or shipped.
The similar police activity of gathering together suspects.
The forcible gathering together of any particular group of people.
The summary to a news bulletin.
An upward curvature or convexity, as in the deck of a vessel.
The finishing of an arrangement.

ety: From round + worm.

s.def: An invertebrate animal of the phylum Nematoda and other similar phyla. Many species of roundworms are parasites.

ety: The verb is derived from Late Middle English rousen (“of a hawk: to shake its feathers”); further etymology unknown. Because many terms of French origin are used in falconry, it has been assumed that the Middle English word is derived from Anglo-Norman or French; however, no satisfactory etymon has been found. The following words have been suggested, but are thought by the Oxford English Dictionary to be unlikely due to the differences in meaning: * Anglo-Norman rëuser, roser, ruser, russer, Mi…

s.def: To cause (something) to be (more) active or to move; to agitate, to stir up.
To provoke (someone) to react (for example, in anger or annoyance); to spur; also, to annoy, to tease.
ex: The emperor is roused by this alarm, and the frontiers of all the French dominions are in danger of being insulted [in] the ensuing campaign.
The words they stopped me from uttering may have been very paltry indeed, hardly words to rouse the rabble.

s.def: Originally chiefly followed by up: to cause (an emotional reaction, a feeling, etc.); to excite, to incite, to stir up.
ex: to rouse the emotions or passions
His pride was roused to double activity by the fear that he had forgotten his dignity.
If Cal had needed any more to rouse his ire, this fact was enough.

s.def: Sometimes followed by up: to disturb (someone) from a state of apathy, comfort, etc.
Sometimes followed by up: to wake (oneself or someone) from deep thought, or rest or sleep; to awaken.
ex: […] I must rouse him from his sleep, / Since none else dare.
"And what ails my apparel, old man?" said Damian, turning sternly on the huntsman, as one who has been hastily and uncivilly roused from a reverie.
Her hunger was soon appeased, all the sooner for the new stimulus of happiness that had roused her from her languor, […]

s.def: To lift up or raise (someone; or something, especially the head).
Sometimes followed by up: to cause (oneself) to be active or alert; to incite, to stir; also, to cause (oneself) to carry out a task, take action, etc.
Of a hawk: to shake (its own) feathers.
Of a person: to stretch (one's own) body.
Chiefly of a bird: to cause (its crest, feathers, etc.) to become stiff or to stand up.

ety: From roust + about.

s.def: An unskilled laborer, especially at an oilfield, at a circus or on a ship.
ex: Then Sísiphos in torment I beheld / being roustabout to a tremendous boulder.
Brooklyn Tony, who had run away from home to be a circus roustabout, became a poster artist and eventually an Abstract Expressionist.
She works in McGregor, North Dakota as a roustabout pusher. That means she and her crew help fix and maintain the drilling sites.

s.def: To work as a roustabout.
ex: When Jack is old and weatherbeat, / Too old to roustabout, / In some rum-shop they’ll let him stop, / At eight bells he’s turned out.
Thereafter, the youth gives many years to aimless wandering about the South and the Middle West. He roustabouts with a carnival […]

ety: The noun is derived from Middle English rout, route (“group of people associated with one another, company; entourage, retinue; army; group of soldiers; group of pirates; large number of people, crowd; throng; group of disreputable people, mob; riot; group of animals; group of objects; proper condition or manner”) [and other forms], from Anglo-Norman route, rute, Middle French rote, route, Old French rote, route, rute (“group of people, company; group of armed people; group of criminals; group…

s.def: A group of people; a crowd, a throng, a troop; in particular (archaic), a group of people accompanying or travelling with someone.
ex: 'Is there anyone in this rout with authority to treat with me?' he asked.

s.def: A group of animals, especially one which is lively or unruly, or made up of wild animals such as wolves; a flock, a herd, a pack.
A group or assortment of snails.
ex: hiruvananthapuram: Routs of snails are invading parts of the city, sending residents into a tizzy, amid fears that they would pose a health hazard
We spot several routs of snails moving around, half buried in the sandy beach.
Researchers in Japan have altered the destiny of a rout of snails by changing the chirality of their shells before birth.

s.def: A group of disorganized things.

A group of (often violent) criminals or gangsters; such people as a class; (more generally) a disorderly and tumultuous crowd, a mob; hence (archaic, preceded by the), the common people as a group, the rabble.
A fashionable assembly; a large evening party, a soirée.
ex: The ancients have always been opposed to them; just as, at routs and dances, elderly beauties to younger.

s.def: A noisy disturbance; also, a disorderly argument or fight, a brawl; (uncountable) disturbance of the peace, commotion, tumult.
ex: Hearing the rout, Dame Gill came out, With a horse whip from the door, She laid it on Jack, And poor Jill's back, Until they both did roar.
"Nay, child! it is not well," I said, / "Among the graves to shout; / To laugh and play among the dead, / And make this noisy rout."

s.def: An illegal assembly of people; specifically, three or more people who have come together intending to do something illegal, and who have taken steps towards this, regarded as more serious than an unlawful assembly but not as serious as a riot; the act of assembling in this manner.
To assemble in a crowd, whether orderly or disorderly; to collect in company.
To cause to move.

ety: From Middle English route, from Old French route, from Latin rupta [via] (literally “a path made by force”). Compare Modern French route. See routine. Further via Latin ruptus related with bankrupt. Unrelated to road.

s.def: A course or way which is traveled or passed.
ex: The route was used so much that it formed a rut.
You need to find a route that you can take between these two obstacles.

s.def: A regular itinerary of stops, or the path followed between these stops, such as for delivery or passenger transportation.
ex: We live near the bus route.
Here is a map of our delivery routes.
The Route 4 bus will arrive on 5th St. at Robinson Ave at 3:30.

s.def: A road or path; often specifically a highway.
ex: Follow Route 49 out of town.

s.def: One of multiple methods or approaches to doing something.
One of the major provinces of imperial China from the Later Jin to the Song, corresponding to the Tang and early Yuan circuits.
ex: Under the director were eight education promotion officials (quanxue yuan), each installed in a “route”(lu,corresponding to the policing ward).

s.def: A specific entry in a router that tells the router how to transmit the data it receives.
A race longer than one mile.
A path that has been secured by a railway signalling system for the passage of a train and locked to prevent any conflicting train movements from taking place.
To direct or divert along a particular course.
ex: All incoming mail was routed through a single office.

s.def: to connect two local area networks, thereby forming an internet.

ety: From route + -er.

s.def: A device that connects local area networks to form a larger internet by, at minimum, selectively passing those datagrams having a destination IP address to the network which is able to deliver them to their destination; a network gateway.
ex: The router was configured to forward packets outside of a certain range of IP addresses to its internet uplink port.

s.def: Any device that directs packets of information using the equivalent of Open Systems Interconnection layer 3 (network layer) information. Most commonly used in reference to Internet Protocol routers.
In integrated circuit or printed circuit board design, an algorithm for adding all wires needed to properly connect all of the placed components while obeying all design rules.
A list and record of instructions that follows a part in a manufacturing process.
Someone who routes or directs items from one location to another.
ex: The router directed the movement of the company's trucks.
When the router receives the package, he places the route number on it as well as on the triplicate part of the attached salescheck.
The system benefits include reduced delivery costs, increased vehicle use, and improved route decision making by dispatchers and routers.

s.def: A plane with a hooked tool protruding far below the sole, for smoothing the bottom of a cavity.
A power tool used in carpentry for cutting grooves.
ex: He made an attractive edge on the table with a router.

s.def: A plane made like a spokeshave, for working the inside edges of circular sashes.
to hollow out or cut using a router power tool.
ex: An alternative is shown in which the carcase ends are grooved by routering.
Routered holes may also be filled with diluted maple syrup (1 part syrup to 9 parts water) to create a sap well for sapsuckers.

ety: Unadapted borrowing from French routine. By surface analysis, route + -ine. Further from Latin rupta via. Compare typologically travel << Latin tripālium, whence also travail, note the inverse semantic vector from a subjective state (toil) to an objective action (journey). Also compare Czech běžný (< běžet), Russian обихо́д (obixód), обихо́дный (obixódnyj) (akin to ходи́ть (xodítʹ)).

s.def: A course of action to be followed regularly; a standard procedure.
A set of normal procedures, often performed mechanically.
ex: Connie was completely robotic and emotionless by age 12; her entire life had become one big routine.

s.def: A set piece of an entertainer's act.
ex: stand-up comedy routine

s.def: A performance, execution of gymnastics for one of the apparatus.
A set of instructions designed to perform a specific task; a subroutine.
Ordinary with nothing to distinguish it from all the others.
ex: Stoke put themselves in a fine position to qualify for the Europa League knockout stage with a routine victory over Maccabi Tel-Aviv in Israel.

s.def: Regular; habitual.
ex: Pepper's forgiven me in the quiet, hurt way women sometimes forgive. She doesn't cry. She doesn't smile either. She's being routine.

s.def: Boringly predictable, monotonous, and unchanging
ex: I found the work pretty routine.

s.def: According to established procedure.

ety: Probably from Middle English *roven, a Midlands variant of Northern Middle English raven (“to wander”), from Old Norse ráfa (“to rove; stray about”). Cognate with Icelandic ráfa (“to wander”), Scots rave (“to wander; stray; roam”).

s.def: To shoot with arrows (at).
To roam, or wander about at random, especially over a wide area.
ex: And a rovin’, a rovin’, a rovin’ I'll go / For a pair of brown eyes
